Srsly Risky Biz: Iranian hacks with Russian characteristics

Presented by

Amberleigh Jack

Producer and Editor

Policy & Intelligence

Tom Uren and Amberleigh Jack talk about the French government attributing freezer hacks to cyber units within the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corp. This surprises Tom, because the hacks were entirely consistent with Russian sabotage operations across Europe.

They also discuss how China’s cyber operators are turning the dial up to 11. Faster, noisier, and stealthier all at the same time, depending upon which particular threat actor you look at.

articles.title: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
articles.context: ” A 26-hour battle The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure
articles.full_text:
As AI model training and distillation increase, AI tokens are becoming a piping hot currency for threat actors.

Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials.

Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, and posted a follow-up report this week. Because of the ongoing investigation, it is not able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits, but advised users to revoke and reapply sensitive environmental variables stored on Railway prior to October 21.

“AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers,” said David Shipley of Beauceron Security. “So-called LLMjacking is expected to displace Cryptojacking as a cheap, scalable way to make money.”

A 26-hour battle

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. They were able to evade filesystem isolation protections and obtain an internal credential that they used to access stored build histories. From there, they retrieved a copy of Railway’s internal source code and analyzed it to identify additional avenues of compromise.

They then exploited another vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship that allowed them to gain even more access to Railway’s infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

In a nearly 26-hour battle, Railway’s engineering team worked 24-7 in shifts and the escalating situation became a “contest of agent speed,” the company explained. The threat actor chained various exploits, moved laterally across multiple systems, and “probed many potential routes, in parallel.” Defenders in turn hardened routes in parallel.

“This was not a single breach followed by a single fix,” Railway wrote.

The threat actors were “fully evicted” on October 21, but over the course of their time in the system, they obtained and decrypted a “subset” of customer variables, roughly 100,000, or “at most” 1.85% of workspaces. They also racked up $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The company is working to reimburse customers, including for charges providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, which included GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway says it reset. The company worked quickly with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe, and others to revoke potentially compromised keys.

In the wake of the attack, customers have been advised to remove public network access to databases; rotate any sensitive variables and keys; check GitHub account audit logs and review all app access; and check audit logs within registries such as Dockerhub.

On its own systems, Railway said it shut down any potentially compromised internal tooling; rolled all keys and “then rerolled them” after validating that intruders had been shut out; moved to a new generation of infrastructure; rebuilt tooling used to run its infrastructure; and added functionality to mass revoke Railway app permissions in the event of suspicious activity in the future.

Why attackers want AI keys

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, Shipley noted; attackers can hit a provider like Railway rather than trying to target one company at a time. That access can then be resold to generate revenue through so-called AI routers, which provide access to models that users otherwise could not afford, or even reach.

This makes that access a hot commodity for tasks like distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs and improve efficiency.

Training one model on another model’s answers at scale takes millions of questions, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, and a single account asking millions of questions stands out. Stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers.

“Think of copying a textbook one page at a time, using library cards that belong to other people,” Dickson explained. Frontier AI is expensive to buy, and the owner of the keys gets the bill while the thief gets cost-free compute.

“It is the 2026 version of cryptomining; [the] same playbook with a different output,” he said.

Managing identities when so many are machine-held

Even though the facts are ugly, Railway deserves credit for a “remarkably candid report,” Dickson emphasized: It owns its own configuration mistake, it admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created, and it commits to telling customers of issues more quickly in the future.

Railway is now moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. That is the right fix, Dickson said, and every platform holding customer secrets should copy it.

“Railway customers should treat every secret stored on the platform as stolen until they have rotated it,” he noted. But that rotation has to beat the thief’s clock; an investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later.

Start with AI provider keys, then rotate cloud, database, and payment credentials, he advised. Check AI provider bills and usage logs for traffic internal teams did not generate, then report any unauthorized charges to Railway. Alert on any call from an unrecognized address.

Further, he said, limit the damage any one key can do. Set hard spending caps and usage alerts on every AI key, and scope each key as narrowly as the provider allows. This really works: In one case Wiz examined, a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief’s traffic throttled.

Non-Railway users, meanwhile, should ask their platform providers two questions: How are my secrets stored, and who can decrypt them? A good standard practice: Issue fewer keys. “No one ever said during a key rotation that they wished they had issued more keys,” Dickson pointed out.

Ultimately, he said, a stolen AI key spends real money, and machines now hold most of the keys. “Protect machine identities like cash, because to a thief, that is exactly what they are,” Dickson urged.

articles.full_text:
You’re driving your new Chinese SUV when the dashboard goes dark. Ten minutes later, your phone rings. A stranger says they’ve got the digital key to your car, and would you like it back? Of course you would. That’ll be $550.

Meanwhile, three men have been charged over a scheme that used deepfakes of company bosses to steal around $130 million. Hear more about what happened, and the simple human trick that can foil the fakes.

All this and more in episode 492 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Danny Palmer.

I'm going to be talking about how 3 men have been charged with using deepfake AI scams to steal millions of dollars from companies around the world.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And I'm going to be discussing how Russian cars are being turned into pumpkins — well, metaphorical pumpkins at least — and why a stranger on the phone is selling the owners their keys back. All this and much more coming up on this episode of Smashing Security. It's not Geoff, Joe. It's an agent. Because your security team isn't just humans anymore. It's humans and AI agents working the same shifts, touching the same systems.

2 kinds of worker on the same team.

And here's the question no one's asking in the budget meeting. Do you actually know whether both of them can do the job?

You trust your analysts because they've got certifications, experience, a CV you have interviewed against.

JOE

That's smashingsecurity.com/hackthebox.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Now, chums, imagine you find yourself in this situation. You've just bought yourself a rather lovely Chinese electric SUV, and you're driving it along, dumpty dumpty dum, singing a little song.

DANNY PALMER

Is that your choice of music? You're driving along. That's what I like to —

GRAHAM CLULEY

I tune into Tumty Tumty Tum FM, as opposed to Tumty Tumty Tum Gold. Of course, I'm not so much into that era. But anyway, you're driving along. Suddenly, the dashboard goes completely dark, and you think, "Oh, this is no good." And you assume it's some kind of glitch because it's scary these days, isn't it? Driving a car and the electrics go. You think, "Oh, can I trust anything?" So you switch off the car and you switch it on again, and up pops on your dashboard a QR code. With a Chinese message telling you to reactivate your car, and you've got one of these newfangled cars, which of course has an app.

DANNY PALMER

Of course.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And you have it on your mobile phone. Of course. And what you discover when you open the app is that your car isn't listed in the app anymore, so you're not able to re-enable it. And ten minutes later, your phone rings, and a stranger says, "Hello, hello, hello. I've got the digital key to your car. Would you like it back?"

DANNY PALMER

Oh, yes, please.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes, please is the obvious answer. But then they ask for 45,000 rubles. Which sounds like an awful lot — well, it is quite a lot. It's $550. And this is happening right now to owners of Li Auto cars in Russia. Li Auto is a Chinese manufacturer of motor vehicles, and this is all according to a story in the Russian outlet Auto News. So here's how all of this works. The key to one of these cars isn't really a key at all. It's actually an account in the app.

DANNY PALMER

So they get in the car by turning on the app. Is that like their keys, basically?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, you do actually get this these days, don't you? You get the ability to lock and unlock your car, or many cars these days, via an app, or turn on the heating.

DANNY PALMER

Yes.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Start the engine, and things like that. So if you control that account, the car thinks that you are the owner rather than maybe the genuine owner. So the criminals aren't hacking into the cars themselves. They're taking over the accounts. And those accounts with these particular cars are linked to a phone number. But you remember I said that these were Chinese SUVs?

Unknown

With the Chinese messaging on the app as well.

GRAHAM CLULEY

That's right. And many of these cars have actually been hardcoded, it turns out, to require, at least for the app, a Chinese phone number. So these cars are often being grey imported into Russia and people are using them, but they don't have a Chinese phone number. So what they do is they rent those Chinese phone numbers online, often through a middleman. So there is a Chinese phone number connected to this, yes. Nobody yet knows how the criminals are breaking into these accounts, and even the owners who feel like they've done everything right to protect themselves seem to be getting hit. And this same scam of basically messing around with people's cars is not actually that new.

Unknown

No.

GRAHAM CLULEY

It hit Li Auto owners in Russia last summer. So, Danny, is there anything which hackers aren't attacking at the moment? I mean, we've seen freezers being attacked. We've seen blood banks being attacked.

Unknown

Yeah.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I was reading a report today of electronic billboards being breached to show porn. What's going on?

Unknown

Yeah, I think that's quite a common trick by pranksters, I think you call them. As we've seen this week, so much is just connected now to the internet and everything is almost hackable. Cars have been connected to the internet in one way or another for at least a decade now. I seem to remember about 10 years ago, there was a story where some ethical hackers managed to, in a test environment, make an internet-connected car basically control the steering.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh my goodness.

DANNY PALMER

10 years ago, not much has changed apparently.

Unknown

There's more internet now on your car, so that's good.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So back in 2025, when these particular attacks first started against the Li Auto cars, the criminals were asking for about 250,000 rubles to get a car back. That's about $3,500.

DANNY PALMER

They've dropped their prices.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, they have. This is interesting, isn't it? So the official fix through the dealers back then cost about 18,000 rubles, which is about $220. And some of those hackers were remotely opening windows and doors and starting engines, almost as if they were taunting the owners.

DANNY PALMER

Like some sort of evil Brum. One for the kids there.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I think you're going to have to explain because Brum was kind of like a bit like Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, wasn't he?

DANNY PALMER

It was live action back in the '90s and there was a model car. It was like an old style, you know, 1920s, '30s car.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes.

DANNY PALMER

And he had headlights that looked like eyes and he went around and had little adventures.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yeah. Anyway, back last year, Russian owners were told how to protect themselves. They were told, look, register your Chinese phone number in your own name. Don't use a middleman. Keep it paid up. So keep on paying for the account. Don't let it expire in any way. Make sure that you don't lose control over that account because the number is what the car's digital key relies upon. The twist this year seems to have been that the attackers have moved on. So the car owners who followed the previous advice, they did everything right. You know, they paid for their Chinese phone number, they registered it in their own name. They're still being hit. And the ransom demand has, as we mentioned, it's crashed in price. So previously, rather than the equivalent of about $3,000, they're asking for $550 instead after they've been immobilised. So I'm always kind of encouraged when the cybercriminals think, oh, market forces, bloody hell, we're gonna have to lower our prices. I mean, that's got to be good news, hasn't it?

Unknown

You'd hope so, because with things like ransomware, it's just been going the other way, is it? I remember when ransomware cost you £500 for an attack, and now you're lucky if it's £5 million.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes. So a story where it's actually reducing is good, but still, your screen on your car is going dark, the climate control stops. Some drivers are saying they can't start their engines at all. Others say that they could still run the car if they used an old-fashioned physical key. My goodness, who starts a car with a key? I think it's a bloody good idea if you keep your key, to be honest. As far as all the reports I've heard, nobody's car has been driven away. But if they are able to remotely unlock it, I suppose there is the possibility if they work out where it's physically located, they could go round and pinch it as well.

Unknown

That is a very interesting concept. Yeah.

GRAHAM CLULEY

But often it's just left sitting there like an expensive paperweight. One of the Russian headlines actually said it's kind of like being turned into Cinderella's pumpkin. So how are the hackers doing this? Well, nobody knows. The founder of the Owners Club thinks the attackers are looking up the VIN, the vehicle identification numbers, in leaked insurance documents and databases to find the owners. He thinks it's unlikely to be a lone hacker because of the need for all of these Chinese SIM card details, the leaked data, and of course, having people to do the ransom negotiation. But reports are also saying that these attacks are mostly happening at night. So it could be just someone's side hustle, for a bit of extra cash. I don't know. The victims, though, they say that Li Auto aren't being helpful. They say the phone number providers aren't being any help either. The company itself, they say they're building a fix that swaps out the requirement for a Chinese phone number for an email address.

Unknown

I mean, that seems like a no-brainer really, because if you bought one of these cars in another country and you have to set up a Chinese phone number on a Chinese phone, that seems like a lot of extra steps.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I wonder if it was an attempt to prevent too much grey importing, to have a little bit more control over who might be selling the cars, to make sure that you went through official distributors instead of— I don't know. I don't know what their thinking was.

Unknown

No, we're not experts on the Russian or Chinese auto industry here.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes, you'll have to listen to another very niche podcast for that, I suspect. Anyway, the advice, of course, is don't pay because paying doesn't actually guarantee you get access back to your car. It looks like dealers are actually able to do this for less money than the blackmailers are requiring. But you should be reporting it to police. And the other piece of advice that's just been given is take screenshots. I guess as evidence as to what's happened.

Unknown

How would you take a screenshot in a car?

GRAHAM CLULEY

You can take screenshots on a car. If you press down the clutch pedal while inserting a thumb down the exhaust pipe — I'm not suggesting people try this. And also you'd have to be a bit like Mr. Tickle to reach so far around.

Unknown

Or is that screenshot on the app?

GRAHAM CLULEY

I suppose screenshot of any messages you might receive, but maybe just a photograph. A shot of the screen in your car, yes, perhaps. If a remote off switch for a car sounds like a brand new problem, it isn't. For instance, back in 2010 in Austin, Texas, there was a dealership there which fitted some of its cars with a little sort of GPS box.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And they had some control over things. So if a buyer of the car fell behind on their payments, the dealer could actually remotely stop the car from starting and could even set off the horn. So then repossession agents could find the car and retrieve it.

DANNY PALMER

While annoying all your neighbours at the exact same time.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes. But from the car dealership's point of view, really handy. Until, of course, the wrong person got hold of the password. And one day what happened was that more than 100 owners of these particular cars found their cars wouldn't start. And in the middle of the night, all over Austin, horns were going off, which is obviously quite a problem. And some owners were disconnecting their batteries just to get some sleep.

DANNY PALMER

Yes, I imagine. And if any of those owners had dogs or their dogs nearby, they wouldn't like it. They'd start barking.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Right. Anyway, it turned out a 20-year-old who'd lost his job at the dealership. This is a familiar story, isn't it? Logged back into the system using a password and went down the customer list.

Unknown

Password still password1 as well, I assume.

GRAHAM CLULEY

All too common. It's that or they haven't reset the password. Now, interestingly, the criminals aren't the only ones with access to the car's off switch of these Li Autos. In May 2025, Li Auto's Russian distributor said it was considering remotely blocking the screens of cars. So they were actually thinking of doing it if those cars had been brought in via grey imports again. So they don't like the idea of these cars being imported into Russia on the sly. And so that summer, Russian dealers claimed that a firmware update was turning some grey import Li Auto cars into bricks.

Unknown

Interesting.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And they worked on an unblock tool to deal with that. So it's pretty tough being the owner of one of these cars in Russia. On one side, you've got a manufacturer who's talked about switching off your screen. On the other hand, you've got criminals who are stealing your digital keys. It's causing all sorts of nuisance. Danny, should manufacturers of anything hold the ability to turn off your device remotely, do you think, on something you've bought?

DANNY PALMER

Sounds like it's asking for trouble. It's the way things are. It's annoying. You don't really need to own anything these days. I mean, my wife recently passed a driving test and bought a car, and it's a Mini, and it's pre-smart stuff. We're not having these problems here, but it's just — this whole thing's like people say, oh, you got your internet-connected fridge and it tells you when your milk's about to run out. Well, I could do that myself by looking in the fridge. There's been a few cases where PlayStation games, the company's gone, oh wait, no, we're taking this game offline now. Then all your stuff is gone.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yeah, I guess so.

DANNY PALMER

Yeah. It's annoying for consumers that this is happening and even more so in the physical realm, I suspect. What has me thinking in this story is there seems to be no indication as to who is conducting this campaign either, which is interesting because you don't often hear about cyberattacks targeting targets in Russia.

GRAHAM CLULEY

You don't too much, do you?

DANNY PALMER

No.

JOE

This episode of Smashing Security is sponsored by Dropzone AI.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to Alert Quiz. Our contestant today is Joe. Joe, are you ready?

JOE

I think so.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Right then. Question 1 for 10 points. What is a security alert?

JOE

It's a flag that something might be wrong.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Correct! Question 2: give me an example.

JOE

Someone's lost their lanyard?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh dear, oh dear, oh dear. Answers I would've accepted include an odd sign-in from abroad or someone clicking a dodgy-looking email. Question 3: what does each alert need before anyone knows that it matters?

JOE

Crumbs. A person pulling evidence from several different tools.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Correct! And when there are more alerts than hours in the day, some of them—

JOE

Get ignored?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Correct! Right, bonus question. What is Dropzone AI?

JOE

Ah, I know this. It's a collective of specialised AI agents that investigates every alert start to finish around the clock using the tools your team already has.

GRAHAM CLULEY

10 bonus points. And what do analysts get when they run Dropzone AI?

JOE

A vague something's up?

GRAHAM CLULEY

No, Joe, that's what they get now. With Dropzone AI, they get a finding with the reasoning and evidence already assembled. It shows its work. So checking a finding becomes a decision rather than a second investigation. And who decides where the agents stop?

GRAHAM CLULEY

The agents?

GRAHAM CLULEY

No, Joe. The team decides where the agents stop, and the analysts own every verdict. Now, final, final question. Finish this quote. Kevin Turnbull, global IT director at Asala Energy, says, with Dropzone, we don't get, this is a problem. We get—

GRAHAM CLULEY

With Dropzone, we don't get, this is a problem. We get, this is a problem, and here's why.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Huzzah! Correct, Joe. You have won the self-guided demo, and what's more, so has everyone who's listening. To watch a real investigation unfold, go to smashingsecurity.com/dropzoneai.

JOE

That's smashingsecurity.com/dropzoneai.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Dropzone AI, reinforcements have arrived.

JOE

Nice demo, but can I swap it for a car?

GRAHAM CLULEY

No, Joe. Danny, what's your story for us this week?

DANNY PALMER

As much as I am loath to admit it, when there are still so many issues around cybersecurity which come down to the basics not being done, it's impossible to ignore how the rise of AI has had an impact on cyberattacks. Because, you know, who would have predicted that cybercriminals would almost immediately latch onto a new technology to do bad things?

GRAHAM CLULEY

As if.

DANNY PALMER

As if. Yeah. I mean, imagine the internet being used for crime, let alone write better, more convincing phishing emails or use ever more readily available deepfake tools to pose as celebrities, CEOs, and other well-known individuals to trick people, right? Who'd have thought that could be a thing? Not possible. Alas, it is the case. And last year alone, it's estimated that fraudsters used audio and video deepfakes to successfully steal over $1.5 billion in total. And that's just the cases we know about.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Hang on, this is just by deepfake audio and video?

DANNY PALMER

Yep, just by deepfakes, $1.5 billion.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Wow, that is astonishing, isn't it? I didn't know it was at that kind of scale.

DANNY PALMER

Yeah, that's just last year. It's likely going to be more this year as well. So yeah, it's tricky out there. And one of the most common methods of this is known as CEO fraud, which I'm sure listeners of Smashing Security don't need me to explain. But just in case, as a quick rundown, as the name suggests, it sees scammers using AI deepfakes to look or sound like the CEO, an executive, or someone else important at a major company, call up another executive or an employee with the voice and the face of the person they're impersonating and say, oh, could you make this urgent business transaction please to this bank account? I mean, it's essentially the evolution of the old business email compromise attacks, which, you know, are very lucrative in themselves. Except in this case, they're not just using email to coerce employees into making payments — they're also using the audio and video as well. Often these requests come with claims that, oh, it's a secret but important deal, so you must not tell anyone about this in order to make sure it goes through. There are two things here that make these work. One is often they work because they're deepfakes of CEOs and other public figures who by their very nature are public-facing, so audio and video of them speaking is out there.

Unknown

Yeah.

DANNY PALMER

And attackers can use that information to do that. I mean, someone could audio deepfake us. Imagine.

GRAHAM CLULEY

The thing is, I'm sure most of our listeners know this, but they are astonishingly convincing these days.

articles.title: Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise
Baker Tilly notifies clients of data breach at third-party provider
articles.context: BleepingComputer did not find any announcements from ransomware groups claiming the attack
articles.full_text:
The Baker Tilly Advisory Group is notifying clients that a data breach has compromised certain personal information about them and their dependents.

The company said the exposed data was stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider Baker Tilly uses to serve clients.

Baker Tilly learned of the incident on September 6 and completed its review of the affected data on October 28, when it identified whose information was involved.

“On September 6, 2026, Baker Tilly became aware of a potential cybersecurity incident involving certain information stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider used by Baker Tilly in connection with services we provide to clients,” reads the notification to customers.

“The unauthorized actor was able to obtain data relating to certain Baker Tilly clients,” the company added.

The breach notification does not provide a count of impacted clients, does not name the service provider, and leaves the specific data types exposed as a placeholder.

Data from the Office of the Texas Attorney General reports that Baker Tilly impacted 10,456 individuals in the state of Texas alone. The portal lists Social Security numbers (SSNs), full names, addresses, and other information as exposed data types.

Baker Tilly is a major accounting firm in the U.S., providing auditing, tax planning, compliance, advisory, and business operations services. Globally, the company operates in 147 countries and reports an annual revenue of $6.8 billion.

After discovering the incident, the company says it took immediate steps to contain it, contracted external experts to investigate, and notified law enforcement authorities.

Furthermore, it says it currently has no evidence of unauthorized activity on its own network, and added that it has no reports of identity theft or fraud linked to the exposure of customer information.

To mitigate the risks arising from the incident, the firm offers affected individuals 24 months of credit and identity monitoring through Experian.

BleepingComputer has contacted Baker Tilly for more information about the data breach, its source, the number of affected customers, and the type of data compromised, but we have not received a reply by the time of publishing.

BleepingComputer did not find any announcements from ransomware groups claiming the attack.

articles.title: ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know
articles.context: Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability
articles.full_text:
A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously.

Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets.

Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX.

Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting.

External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse. Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt.

Here, we share our observations of how attackers are using AI-powered red team tools, along with our recommendations for how defenders can mitigate.

Why Is ARTEX Such an Effective Tool for Attackers?

ARTEX and other red-teaming platforms are free, quick to deploy and need little more than access to a large language model (LLM).

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration testing framework first published in mid-2026. It has been widely forked since.

Attackers can use ARTEX to evaluate responses, adapt when something fails and keep pursuing their objective. They can target the identity workflows and APIs that organizations expose to the internet, and then use the associated credentials and trust relationships to reach the cloud.

AI-Powered Red Teaming and Pentesting Ecosystem Infrastructure

As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing hosts running CyberStrikeAI and 609 running ARTEX. Notably, 21 hosts were running both at the same time.

Unit 42 analyzed 14 tools across the pentesting and red-teaming tool ecosystem, highlighting 12 emerging tools alongside CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX.

These tools can be broken down into four categories of AI assisted red team activities.

Category

Tools

Goal

Reconnaissance and attack-surface management

ARL, ARL-Next, Scope Sentry, Nemo, XingRin, OpenEASD

Identify what assets exist, what is exposed and what changes

Agent-led testing and vulnerability hunting

CyberStrikeAI, ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, AutoHunter

Manage what should be investigated and how the system can act on it

Source-code auditing and verification

DeepAudit, AIxVuln

Identify where source code might be vulnerable and what supports that finding

AI-system security assessment

AI-Infra-Guard

Identify if AI infrastructure, agents, tools and model interfaces are vulnerable or unreliable

Table 1. Tool categories.

Implications For Defenders

Defenders should be aware of the following implications of AI-powered red teaming platforms:

Lowered Skill Floor for Attackers

Adversaries no longer require specialized tradecraft to execute multi-stage, adaptive penetration testing.

Off-the-shelf tooling combined with LLMs like DeepSeek allows financially motivated actors to launch and manage dozens of complex, concurrent network intrusions for minimal compute cost.

Risk of Internet-Exposed Assets

Any internet-exposed asset, regardless of organizational size or sector, is equally likely to be impacted by automated, persistent intrusion attempts.

Attackers using the autonomous AI penetration testing framework ARTEX are turning public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day. Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability.

Because these autonomous platforms cannot target what they cannot find, continuous discovery and mitigation of exposed edge assets remains an effective barrier against automated campaigns.

Proactive AI Adoption Helps Defenders

Autonomous testing frameworks rely on foundational LLM reasoning patterns. Therefore, there is some predictability to AI-powered adversary tooling.

Security teams do not need to guess an agent's methodology; they can deploy identical open-weight offensive frameworks internally to surface, validate and remediate vulnerable exposure before external agents identify them.

Defenders Benefit From Tracking Ecosystem Shifts

The rapid adoption curve of tools in this ecosystem highlights how quickly operational trends can shift. Keeping an eye on these developments provides practical defensive advantages:

Observing emerging agent-led frameworks allows teams to test new capabilities early in controlled environments.

Monitoring the infrastructure hosting these tools makes it possible to update perimeter blocks before active targeting begins.

Current AI-Powered Frameworks Are Noisy

Current autonomous frameworks prioritize rapid trial-and-error over stealth. In our study of a tool called Cairn, it generated hundreds of thousands of noisy, high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP address.

Organizations with unified perimeter telemetry and centralized logging can readily distinguish this brute-force agentic traffic from legitimate users and block campaigns at the network edge before exploitation occurs.

Defensive Deception Could Help

LLM-driven testing tools use target responses as context for follow up actions.

Defenders may be able to take advantage of this to trick attackers using AI-powered red teaming tools into wasting resources.

When a target serves identical, generic error codes or enforces silent connection throttling, an AI agent lacks the contextual cues needed to adapt. Deprived of environmental feedback, autonomous loops burn context windows and compute budgets on dead ends.

Recognizing an AI-Driven Operator

ARTEX is forked and modified constantly. Furthermore, attackers rotate infrastructure quickly, so indicators lose value fast. How the operator behaves is more durable, and the behavior across our observations consistently pointed to an automated planner reacting to what it sees. Table 2 shows the hallmarks of this behavior.

Hallmark

What We Observed

Think-then-act cadence

Bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25–31 seconds, consistent with an agent waiting on a model inference call

Machine speed

Pivots within about one minute of a credential download. More than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes

Spec-driven targeting

Routes from downloaded OpenAPI specifications and source maps targeted almost immediately

Self-correction

Failed requests (HTTP 422) adjusted and retried successfully moments later

Checking its own work

A GET to the same path after almost every successful write. Write-then-delete tests on storage buckets.

Canary inputs

Bogus usernames before real ones, and placeholder values such as evil[.]com, test@example[.]com and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12

Parallel targeting

An application delivery controller, more than a dozen VPN appliances, a NAS device, workforce identity and cloud ports attacked within the same hour

Recheck loops

Polling every 48 seconds for three days, and attack sequences replayed identically about 30 seconds apart

Table 2. Behavioral hallmarks of ARTEX-driven activity observed by Unit 42.

Any one of these traits could come from an unusually configured tool or a person testing an API by hand. Seen together, they point to autonomous tooling.

Despite the autonomous tooling, humans were not entirely absent from the attacks we observed. In one engagement, the attacker switched from scripted clients to a desktop browser for the password reset and first token request. This suggests a human in the loop, or browser automation, for the most sensitive steps.

Conclusion and Mitigations for ARTEX Attacks

AI-driven tooling is not inventing new attacks. Self-service abuse, exposed APIs and stored credentials are long-standing weak points.

What has changed is the pace and the persistence. An ARTEX operator can test every exposed workflow in parallel and switch routes within minutes of being blocked. It can act on a stolen credential within a minute of finding it.

Because the framework is open source and widely forked, indicator-based detection will not keep up.

Defenders who remove machine-readable attack maps, require authentication everywhere and build detections around operator behavior will be best placed to stop an AI-assisted attacker.

Autonomous tooling probes faster than people can review alerts. Defenses need to block by default and remove the credentials these tools are looking for. Organizations should:

Remove public attack maps. Take OpenAPI specifications, source maps and configuration files containing tokens or client IDs off internet-facing applications.

Reduce and understand your organization’s public footprint. Certificate transparency can create target lists for threat actors. In cloud environments, it is vital to understand if host fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are public knowledge. Consider private certificate authorities to limit information disclosure and locking origin traffic to content delivery network (CDN)-only ingress where possible.

Require authentication on every write endpoint, including development and staging APIs.

Harden self-service flows. Rate-limit and bot-protect registration, password reset and verification code endpoints. Remove unauthenticated account-existence checks.

Protect federated identities. Block local passwords for workforce accounts in customer and partner identity providers, and make sure a password reset can never unlink a federated identity.

Get credentials out of reach. Replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access, keep administrator credentials out of provisioning records and move function secrets to a secrets manager.

Enforce least privilege for workload roles and any function that can create roles, keys or tokens.

Hunt for behavior, not just indicators. Look for:

Canary usernames in identity provider logs

First use of a cloud key from a new IP address

Write-then-delete storage tests

Early-phase probing that precedes a later intrusion

articles.title: Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations
articles.context: Related Articles: Ransomware recovery is now a client retention metric How to secure RMM software: 8 controls MSPs should test Critical ScreenConnect flaw now actively exploited...
articles.full_text:
Update 11/11/26: Added additional information from ConnectWise and Huntress.

ConnectWise is investigating an active malware campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) that uses compromised ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients to customer devices.

As part of its investigation, ConnectWise has disabled five third-party ScreenConnect extensions across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution, warning that they may be associated with the attacks.

The campaign was first discovered Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Huntress, which says it has identified six compromised MSPs and 286 affected endpoints across 47 organizations, and that the number of victims continues to rise.

"Our SOC is working an active campaign that started around 17:47 UTC today targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances," Huntress posted to Reddit.

"We are currently tracking 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints, and those numbers are climbing. ConnectWise is engaged and working this with us."

ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices.

According to Huntress, attackers are using ScreenConnect's Run Command functionality to deploy rogue ScreenConnect clients on managed endpoints, providing remote access outside of the legitimate MSP's ScreenConnect environment.

The researchers also warned of a potentially more dangerous technique in which attackers can compromise an MSP technician's workstation when they initiate a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device.

Spike Brandt, Principal Threat Intelligence Incident Commander at Huntress, told BleepingComputer that the activity appears to involve abusing legitimate functionality rather than exploiting a software vulnerability.

"This appears to be abuse of legitimate functionality, aided using custom-built tooling that is, in some cases, compiled on the fly on the victim’s computer," Brandt told BleepingComputer.

"We have no information about how a “patient zero” computer or machine would have initiated this attack."

Huntress said it began receiving alerts when rogue ScreenConnect clients appeared on monitored endpoints and subsequently retrieved attacker scripts that were still accessible to analyze how the attacks worked.

However, the precise mechanism allowing malware to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation has not been publicly explained.

ConnectWise disables third-party extensions

In a security advisory published Wednesday night, ConnectWise confirmed unauthorized access to ScreenConnect partner accounts and the installation of unauthorized remote-access software in customer environments.

As part of its investigation, the company discovered five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with the attacks and disabled them across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution.

ScreenConnect extensions are installed through its built-in Extensions marketplace via the ScreenConnect administration interface.

The extensions are:

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

"Our initial assessment leads us to suspect the threat actor deployed additional remote-access software through independent 3rd party extensions that partners may have added to their environments," ConnectWise said.

The company stressed that having these extensions installed does not necessarily mean that a network was compromised and that the attacks remain under investigation.

"Disabling these 3rd party extensions is a precautionary containment measure. It does not establish that unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already present on affected devices has been removed," explained ConnectWise

While ConnectWise has disabled the extensions in affected cloud-hosted environments, it warned that on-premises ScreenConnect customers must disable them manually, as the company cannot do so from their end.

Partners were also instructed not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance is available.

ConnectWise warned that disabling the extensions does not remove malicious software, persistence mechanisms, or unauthorized access that attackers may have already established on compromised endpoints.

The company advised partners to review authentication logs, extension installation records, administrative activity, Run Command history, and Toolbox records for suspicious activity.

It also urged technicians to avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially compromised devices and instead use separate security tools to investigate.

ConnectWise also said it has received reports of technician workstations being compromised during interactive ScreenConnect sessions, but these reports are still being confirmed.

The company added that it has no reason to believe partners that have not deployed the five identified extensions are impacted by this incident, but encouraged all partners to remain on heightened alert.

Huntress has not determined how the attackers are gaining access to affected MSP environments, but says its current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions.

Huntress also warned that sequential identifiers used by the attackers suggest additional MSPs may have been previously compromised.

"Sequential attacker-assigned tags suggest other MSPs may have been compromised earlier, so ScreenConnect users should check their Run Command history even if they haven’t received alerts," Huntress told BleepingComputer.

Huntress also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations identify malicious activity, including rogue ScreenConnect client IDs and infrastructure used by the attackers.

The indicators include:

Attacker relay: 185.99.255[.]28 (hostname: screen)

C2 domains: newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org

Possible additional C2: cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com

Secondary C2: sc.payproofkit[.]com (155.94.150[.]39, hostname: WIN-FB5CKHMU4E1)

Stager: hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4

Rogue ScreenConnect client IDs: 2588ef5c15954b10, ed630cc2c873b091

Installer pattern: /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi?...&c=Exploited<N>

Attacker name: Addmin

Files: Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, Run-Lateral-Full.bat

The researchers are urging MSPs to review their environments for signs of compromise and avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints.

Huntress also told BleepingComputer that its researchers have contacted ConnectWise, the VPS provider hosting the attacker's infrastructure, cloud providers whose dynamic DNS services were used in the attacks, and the broader MSP community.

Earlier malware activity linked to rogue ScreenConnect identifier

BleepingComputer found an earlier malicious batch script that references one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs listed by Huntress, suggesting that the ID was used in malicious activity months before the current attacks were disclosed.

The script, named SSA-2026-STATEMENT-15518787.bat (VirusTotal), appears to impersonate a Social Security Administration statement and was first uploaded to VirusTotal on July 25, 2026.

The batch file attempts to add Microsoft Defender exclusions and creates persistence through the Windows Startup folder and the Run registry key.

It then contacts amexsafekeyupdate.com to retrieve installation commands for two separate installers.

VirusTotal sandbox activity associated with the sample includes downloads of ScreenConnect MSI installers from cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com and cyberrexdesign.screenconnect[.]com, with cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com also listed by Huntress as a possible C2 domain.

After launching the second installer, the script uses PowerShell to search running processes and Windows services for ed630cc2c873b091, one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs identified by Huntress.

If the identifier is found, the script considers the installation successful and sends a notification to the attackers through Telegram.

The earlier script also appears designed for a different distribution campaign, with its Social Security-themed filename suggesting it may have been used in phishing attacks.

Asked about the earlier activity, Huntress declined to comment on the specific July incident but said it has observed a significant increase in attacks using legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software as an initial payload in 2026.

The relationship between the July malware activity and the current ScreenConnect attacks remains unclear.

articles.title: Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack
AI Pentest Tool AntiFox Abused To Steal AWS Credentials
articles.context: In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Arctic Wolf saw attackers use the AntiFox pentest platform to hit IIS servers and AWS accounts.

Arctic Wolf Labs has published research on attackers using AntiFox, an open-source, Chinese-language agentic penetration testing platform. These frameworks chain attack steps together with little human effort. In several intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to confirmed attacks on internet-facing web services and the AWS environments behind them.

Two entry points showed up. In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability. In others, they started with a valid AWS credential obtained by means nobody knows.

“Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks, including AntiFox, from public cloud infrastructure.” states the report published by Arctic Wolf, “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.”

The IIS attacks followed a similar pattern. The IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, created an ASPX web shell and then ran commands to gather information about the system. The attackers checked the user account, listed files in the application folder, reviewed file permissions using icacls and tested whether they could write files to the website’s main folder.

They then used PowerShell to read the web.config file, looking for database connection details and application settings. They also checked folders containing debug and error logs. Using credentials found in the configuration file, they tried to connect to an internal production database. Finally, they copied configuration files and logs into an upload folder that could be accessed through the website.

The AWS attacks moved quickly. AntiFox used valid IAM accounts and, in some cases, an assumed EC2 role. The attackers first checked their identity and permissions within AWS. They used commands such as GetCallerIdentity, GetUser, ListUsers, ListRoles, ListPolicies and ListKeys to discover available accounts, roles, policies and access keys. They also tried to obtain an authorization token for Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).

In one intrusion, the source cycled through several AWS identities and sent hundreds of requests in about half an hour.

“The activity then rapidly enumerated services across the affected AWS environments, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock, using List, Get, and Describe operations.” continues the report. “After authorization failures, the activity continued across other services and concentrated on resources that remained accessible.”

Most requests came back as AccessDenied, but a few worked, and the attackers kept going where the doors were open.

Some sequences ended with a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Others focused on S3, listing buckets, objects and versions, reading objects, then copying and deleting them. Nobody has to stay awake for that kind of persistence, which is the whole point of the tool.

Arctic Wolf’s concern is simple. These frameworks make penetration testing techniques easier to reach for attackers, and they make those techniques faster and more consistent in live attacks.

For hunting, start with AWS activity coming from hosting providers the identity has never used. Look for one IP address using many access keys, users or roles in a short time, and for fast runs of List, Get and Describe calls across unrelated services, especially from Boto3 or Botocore. Check GuardDuty for odd IAM user behavior, credential access, discovery and unusual calls from hosting networks.

On the Windows side, watch for w3wp.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, whoami.exe, icacls.exe or archive tools. Look for new .aspx files in upload, temporary and image-conversion folders, and for config or log files saved there under .txt or image extensions. PowerShell commands that read WebConfigurationManager, ConnectionStrings or AppSettings deserve a close look, and so does any AWS activity that starts soon after.

Organizations should enable AWS CloudTrail logging and monitor access to sensitive S3 storage. They should also use S3 versioning and Object Lock to protect important data from deletion. Alerts should flag suspicious access to stored secrets, especially when it follows unusual account activity.

Companies should identify all internet-facing applications and prioritize patching and protecting file upload, conversion and document-processing services. If an IIS process launches an unexpected command shell, administrators should isolate the server, preserve logs and forensic evidence, remove malicious files and change all exposed credentials.

They should also revoke compromised AWS sessions and access keys, enforce IMDSv2 and apply least-privilege permissions to limit what applications can access. As Arctic Wolf warns, a series of mostly denied requests does not mean the attack was unsuccessful.

Pierluigi Paganini

articles.title: Notion says Fireworks breach exposed customer AI chat transcripts
articles.context: Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace...
articles.full_text:
Notion, the digital workspace platform, disclosed that a security breach at its AI infrastructure provider, Fireworks AI, exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces.

The disclosure comes shortly after Fireworks AI confirmed that an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers.

Fireworks AI experienced another breach in early October, when hackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts.

Notion learned about the exposed chat transcripts after receiving an alert from Fireworks on November 2 about an exposed dataset that contained only synthetic test data.

Notion responded by cutting off traffic to Fireworks, deleting all data from the vendor’s systems, and halting training runs by November 3.

However, Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed, including that of Notion users.

Notion is a cloud-based workspace used for note-taking, document creation, internal wikis, project management, and task tracking. It includes an AI assistant that can answer questions, summarize content, and help draft text.

Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace administrators visibility into how their teams use AI.

The exposed transcripts came from the Insights dataset specifically, which has now been disabled.

“Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable,” Notion stated in an update.

"Unattributable means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.”

Notion has also published a FAQ page about the incident, highlighting that Fireworks had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data.

According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident. Potentially affected workspace owners should review the data through Security incident review in Notion’s desktop web interface and share a link with members that lets them download their own transcripts.

Notion advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys, or other credentials entered into affected chats.

If neither a user nor their workspace owner has received a notice, Notion says no action is needed for now, and they are most likely not part of the impacted subset.

articles.title: WhiteArmor Demands $5 Million from Maersk, Claims Theft of 100GB of Data
articles.context: The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect...
articles.full_text:
Maersk confirms a data breach involving a legacy system, while WhiteArmor claims 100GB of stolen data and demands a $5 million ransom.

A.P. Moller Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, says it identified an IT security incident involving unauthorized access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, one inherited from a previous acquisition.

“Maersk has identified an IT security incident involving unauthorised access and data extraction from one of our local legacy systems from a previous acquisition.” reads the statement published by Maersk on November 11. “Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI.”

According to Maersk, its cyber security team started a full investigation as soon as it found the problem, and it’s still going. The company says swift action secured the affected system. Its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it says the incident is isolated to that one local system.

Maersk has found no sign that other Maersk systems were affected, or the customer and partner systems that connect to it through integrations such as APIs and EDI. It doesn’t expect disruption for customers, who can book and manage shipments as usual. It promises updates and says it will inform any affected parties if it finds a need to.

Maersk didn’t name the system, the type of data or the date of the intrusion. However, the cybercrime group WhiteArmor added the company to its Tor data leak site:

WhiteArmor demanded a $5 million ransom in Bitcoin, giving Maersk 30 days to pay. The group claims to have stolen about 100 GB of data from the OCF/LF Logistics platform, which supports logistics and supply chain operations.

“”Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world’s largest consumer brands,” states the leak site. “Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA.””

Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the company that developed the platform, from the Li & Fung Group in 2022. This could match Maersk’s reference to an old system inherited through an acquisition, although the company has not confirmed this connection.

According to the attackers, the stolen data includes nearly 30,000 driver records, passwords stored in plain text, 33 super admin accounts and signed delivery receipts. The group also claims to have stolen inventory records, purchase orders, advance shipping notices and 27,842 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEI numbers. These details come from the attackers and have not been independently verified. Maersk’s statement does not confirm their claims. WhiteArmor also tried to justify its demand, saying the $5 million ransom represents roughly four hours of revenue for the logistics business.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.” concludes the statement. “We will keep customers updated as more relevant information becomes available, and if we identify any need to inform impacted parties of any further findings, we will do so.”

The scale of Maersk’s operations explains why this incident matters. A.P. Moller-Maersk is one of the world’s largest integrated shipping and logistics companies, playing a major role in global trade and supply chains. It operates around 700 container ships, representing approximately 13.5% of global container fleet capacity, and manages 60 terminals across 35 countries. The company employs about 100,000 people in 130 countries and provides services covering ocean shipping, port operations, warehousing, customs clearance and end-to-end supply chain management.

Maersk reported approximately $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit in 2025. Its global reach and reliance on interconnected IT systems make cybersecurity a major concern. A breach involving even an older, locally operated platform could expose sensitive business and personal information, including data belonging to drivers, customers and logistics partners, even if the company’s main systems remain unaffected.

In 2017, NotPetya forced the company to reinstall more than 4,000 servers and 45,000 workstations from scratch. It operated without IT for ten days and took damages of up to $300 million.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, ransomware)

articles.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
articles.context: When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process
articles.full_text:
In this article

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Observed attack chains

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

Mitigation and protection guidance

References

Learn More

Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block.

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it.

To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.

GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it.

Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself.

Outbound-only connections. The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions. The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection. Inbound firewall rules do not see this traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.

Built-in evasion and persistence. The deployment script can rename the process, stage files in memory-backed directories, and install persistence that survives a reboot, without additional development by the threat actor.

The same relay model that supports legitimate remote administration also gives threat actors a way to maintain access without operating dedicated C2 infrastructure. Once GSocket runs on a compromised server, the server and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an end-to-end encrypted channel.

Figure 1: After code execution on an internet-facing application, GSocket is deployed and both ends connect outward to the relay.

Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows that this activity is not limited to a single compromise. From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

Figure 2: Growth in GSocket-related detections from March to August, measured against the March baseline.

Web applications and hosting accounted for 87.1% of attributable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint incidents in the analysed telemetry. Within that group, PHP web applications and cPanel hosting represented 63.9% of incidents and Apache represented 24.3% (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Distribution of GSocket-related incidents by application category. PHP web applications and Apache account for most incidents within the web applications and hosting group.

Education and research accounted for the largest share of affected organizations (30.7%), followed by technology and telecommunications (22.9%).

Figure 4: Distribution of affected organizations by sector.

These figures reflect the share of affected organizations and do not indicate that threat actors selected these sectors deliberately. Exposure is the more likely factor: academic institutions often run large, decentralized web estates maintained outside central IT, which are harder to inventory and patch.

Observed attack chains

The RCE-based intrusions in this analysis followed a similar sequence after initial access. Threat actors compromised an internet-facing application, profiled the host, transferred and concealed the relay tooling, and used the resulting channel for command and control. Some intrusions also included persistence and privilege escalation. Figure 5 combines these behaviours into a generalized attack chain. Not every stage occurred in every intrusion.

Figure 5: Generalized GSocket attack chain observed across RCE-based intrusions, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

Initial access and deployment: Threat actors exploited internet-facing web applications and used curl to download and execute a remote script. The script profiled the host, selected a GSocket client matching the system architecture, staged it in writable or memory-backed paths such as /dev/shm, and established encrypted outbound command and control through the Global Socket Relay Network.

Figure 6: Encoded RCE command executed through a vulnerable PHP application.

Defense evasion and persistence: Threat actors disguised GSocket with kernel-thread-like process names, persisted through cron, systemd, shell profiles, watchdogs, and redundant copies, then removed staging files and other deployment indicators.

Figure 7: Kernel thread names used to disguise the GSocket process. Figure 8: Persistence entries created during GSocket deployment.

Privilege escalation: After gaining execution as the web-service account, in few observed incidents, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284, one of the recent Linux kernel vulnerabilities also known as Dirty Frag, to elevate privileges to root.

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

GSocket identifies endpoints by a shared secret instead of an IP address or hostname. During installation, the deployment script typically generates a random secret and writes it to standard output. The threat actor can choose to read the secret from the console, redirect it to a temporary file and retrieve the file before is deleted, or have it delivered through a supported notification channel, such as Telegram (configured with GS_TG_TOKEN and GS_TG_CHATID), Discord, or a webhook. With this secret, the operator can reconnect later from any compatible GSocket client, without knowing the victim’s IP address, hostname, or network location.

A traditional reverse shell connects to a threat actor-controlled IP address written into the payload. GSocket instead derives its connection identifier and authentication material from the shared secret. The compromised host and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network (GSRN), which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session. Neither endpoint needs a public IP address, an inbound listener, or a permissive inbound firewall rule.

As a result, blocking an IP address or domain is unlikely to cut off access. The connection relies on a shared relay service, outbound traffic that is commonly permitted, and a secret that does not need to be hardcoded in the payload. Anyone with the shared secret can reconnect through the relay without knowing the compromised host’s IP address or hostname.

Mitigation and protection guidance

For an affected Linux server, remediation should address both the initial compromise and the GSocket deployment.

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Remediate the host as well as the vulnerability. Do not treat application patching as complete remediation. Investigate and remove the GSocket client, associated persistence, and staged files, then verify that outbound connections to the relay infrastructure have stopped

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Constrain outbound traffic. Apply deny-by-default egress rules, allow only required destinations, and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.

Harden the host runtime. Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable where feasible, and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.

Audit persistence surfaces. Review cron entries, systemd units with plausible service names, and shell startup files. Persistence is often layered across several mechanisms, so stopping the running process alone does not remove access.

Prioritize local privilege-escalation patching on internet-facing servers. In the analyzed activity, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284 to escalate from the web-service account to root. Separately, Microsoft FORGE Lab recently documented 59 Linux kernel bug reports, including eight vulnerabilities for which researchers demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled environments.

Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux. Keep real-time and cloud-delivered protection enabled, with behavior monitoring for anomalous child processes of web services and masqueraded process identities.

Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint provides visibility into activity associated with GSocket-related Linux intrusions, including suspicious shell execution, payload delivery, persistence, defense evasion, and remote communication. The alerts below were observed in the analyzed telemetry. An individual alert does not establish the initial access method or confirm that every stage of an intrusion succeeded.
