articles.title: October 2026 Cyber Threat Landscape: Record Ransomware, Rising GenAI Risk and an AI-Powered Newcomer
articles.context: Together, these findings reinforce Check Point’s prevention-first view: organizations need AI-powered security, consistent visibility and shared intelligence across the full...
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways

Organizations experienced 2,550 weekly cyber attacks on average in October, down 9% month over month but up 32% year over year.

Education remained the most targeted sector, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, a 33% year-over-year increase, as all 23 tracked sectors saw double digit growth compared to last year.

Europe recorded the sharpest regional rise at 39% year over year, while Africa faced the highest volume at 3,834 weekly attacks per organization.

One in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools.

One in every 128 emails was classified as phishing, down from 1 in 91 in September; 79% of phishing emails contained links.

A total of 1,063 ransomware attacks were reported, the highest in recent years, and 35% more than in October 2025.

New n0n extortion group enters top 3 within a month after initial operation, relying heavily on AI-assisted tooling

October’s data shows a more mixed picture. Weekly attack volumes eased from September and phishing became less frequent, but attacks remain one third higher than a year ago, high-risk GenAI prompts continued to rise, and ransomware reached a record 1,063 reported attacks, with a new actor entering the top three. Together, these findings reinforce Check Point’s prevention-first view: organizations need AI-powered security, consistent visibility and shared intelligence across the full attack surface to reduce risk before it becomes business impact.

Global Cyber Attacks Ease from September but Stay Well Above Last Year

Organizations experienced an average of 2,550 cyber attacks per week in October 2026. That represents a 9% decrease from September, but still a 32% increase compared to October 2025. The monthly dip should not be read as a change in direction: attack levels remain roughly a third higher than a year ago, making resilience, exposure reduction and prevention increasingly important across networks, cloud, endpoints, email and AI services.

Education Still Faces the Highest Attack Volume While Agriculture Surges

Education remained the most targeted industry in October, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, up 33% year over year. The sector continues to face far more attacks than any other, likely reflecting the broad user base and open digital environments of schools, universities and research institutions.

Agriculture ranked second with 3,218 weekly attacks per organization, a 93% increase year over year, closely followed by Telecommunications with 3,068, up 19%. Notably, all tracked sectors recorded a double digit growth from last year, with several highly critical sectors such as Government, Energy & Utilities and Healthcare & Medical also placing in the top half of the ranking. These figures show sustained pressure on sectors with broad user bases, essential services and complex digital environments.

Africa Leads in Volume as Europe Records the Sharpest Increase

Africa recorded the highest regional attack volume in October and climbed back to top place for the first time since September 2025, averaging 3,834 weekly attacks per organization, up 38% year over year. Latin America ranked second at 3,483 weekly attacks, followed by APAC at 3,436. Europe experienced the highest rate of growth, with attacks increasing 39% compared to October 2025. North America also rose sharply, up 33% year over year. Although Europe’s overall volume remains lower than that of the leading regions, it recorded the fastest growth of any region, signaling an intensifying threat environment for organizations there.

GenAI Risk Keeps Rising

In October, 1 in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools. A further 12% of prompts contained potentially sensitive information, keeping data exposure a mainstream governance concern. The global high-risk rate has risen steadily, from 2.3% (1 in 43) in August to 2.5% (1 in 39) in September and 2.9% (1 in 35) in October. The average user generated 91 prompts during the month, and each organization used an average of seven tools. With the risk of data leakage via prompts on the rise, it is increasingly important to understand what employees share, where it is processed and which controls apply.

Latin America recorded the highest regional rate of high-risk prompts at 1 in 26 (3.8%), above the global average. North America followed at 1 in 30 (3.3%) and APAC at 1 in 40 (2.5%). Given the average usage per user, this means that across the globe each user is likely submitting between 2 and 4 prompts which might expose sensitive data per month.

By industry, Business Services had the highest high-risk exposure rate at 5.4%, or 1 in every 19 prompts – almost double the global average. Government followed at 4.6% and Financial Services at 4.5%, with Healthcare & Medical and Information Technology also above the global average. These sectors routinely handle client, financial, citizen and patient information, which helps explain their greater exposure.

Sensitive Data Exposure Spans Core Business Information

Financial Data was the most common sensitive-data category, observed in GenAI prompts at 71% of organizations. Legal and Regulatory data and Network and IT Infrastructure followed at 70% each, Employee and HR data at 67%, and personally identifiable information at 62%. These percentages reflect the share of organizations where each category was observed, not the share of prompts. Network and IT Infrastructure information, such as hardware and network configurations and IP addresses, could give attackers valuable insight into an organization’s internal environment if exposed.

Email Phishing Risk Declines from September

One in every 128 emails, or 0.78%, was classified as phishing in October, down from 1 in 91 (1.10%) in September. Among phishing emails, 79% contained links and 14% contained attachments, confirming malicious links as the primary delivery method. Some phishing emails contained neither and relied on social engineering alone. Although phishing was slightly less frequent than in September, the heavy reliance on links underlines the importance of checking URLs before users click.

North America recorded the highest regional phishing rate, with 1 in 123 emails, or 0.81%, classified as malicious.

By industry, Construction & Engineering had the highest rate at 1.72% (1 in 58 emails), reflecting more than double the global average risk for phishing emails to employees in this sector. Real Estate, Rentals & Leasing followed at 1.05% (1 in 96), and Associations & Nonprofits at 0.97%(1 in 103..

Ransomware Climbs 35% Year over Year

* Ransomware data is drawn from double-extortion groups’ public “shame sites.” Although these sources have inherent biases, they provide useful insight into the ransomware landscape.

A total of 1,063 ransomware attacks were reported in October, representing a 35% increase compared with October 2025, and is the highest number reported to date. Business Services was the most targeted industry, accounting for 31.5% of reported victims. Consumer Goods & Services followed at 14.9%, with Industrial Manufacturing at 11.6%. Because business services providers often hold data or system access on behalf of multiple clients, a single incident can have consequences that extend beyond the organization itself.

North America was the most affected region, accounting for 48% of reported ransomware incidents, followed by Europe at 22% and APAC at 18%. The United States accounted for 44.3% of reported victims, substantially ahead of Germany at 5.2% and Canada at 4.0%. These figures show where publicly claimed victims are concentrated, rather than the level of risk faced by an individual organization in each country.

The Gentlemen Leads the Ransomware Rankings as n0n Enters the Top Three

The Gentlemen was the most prevalent ransomware group in October, responsible for 13% of published attacks. Qilin followed with 12%, while n0n accounted for 8%, entering the top three only one month after appearing for the first time, and quadrupling its monthly share of published victims. The number of active groups has remained stable over the past three months, as new groups became active while others did not show continuous operations.

The Gentlemen: A fast-growing Ransomware-as-a-Service operation founded in mid-2025. It operates as both a RaaS provider and an Initial Access Broker, offering affiliates access to approximately 14,000 pre-exploited FortiGate devices, and supports Windows, Linux and ESXi environments.

Qilin: An established Ransomware-as-a-Service group with victim disclosures dating back to 2022. It provides affiliates with encryption, negotiation and support infrastructure, and has significantly increased its victim listings since March 2025.

n0n: A data-theft and extortion operation that emerged in September 2026 and had claimed more than 170 victims by early November. Its operators made extensive use of AI-assisted tooling, and initial access in observed cases relied on weak or stolen credentials rather than exploited vulnerabilities.

What October Tells Us

October’s figures show the average cyber risk easing month over month but remaining high year over year. Weekly attacks per organization fell 9% from September, and phishing became less frequent, yet attack rates are up in every region and industry compared with last year, high-risk GenAI prompts exposing organizations to data leakage continued to rise, and ransomware remained well above last year’s level and reached a new all time high. The quick rise of n0n, whose operators relied heavily on commercial generative-AI platforms, illustrates how adoption of AI tools accelerates and amplifies the operations and threats posed by attackers.

Organizations should focus on reducing exposure early, before attackers can act on it. Check Point’s prevention-first approach brings together AI-powered protection, shared intelligence and consistent governance across hybrid networks, cloud environments, digital workspaces and AI systems. As established and emerging risks converge, a unified security architecture can help teams prevent threats earlier, reduce complexity and secure AI adoption with greater confidence.

articles.title: Rewriting less than 10 neurons in an LLM can turn it into a sleeper backdoor
articles.context: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required.

Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper. It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it.

“The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.”

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post, said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models.

Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor

The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output.

The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios.

The technique also worked against Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, suggesting that it is not limited to a single model, the researchers wrote in the blog post.

The trigger does not have to be a malicious instruction. According to Microsoft Research, it can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in an agent’s context.

The researchers said Lazarus differs from prompt injection because it changes the model’s underlying weights rather than attempting to manipulate its behavior through instructions supplied in a prompt.

Microsoft Research said the technique requires no model training. Its researchers described it as an inference-compute attack, meaning a machine with enough memory to run a model has sufficient resources to implant the backdoor.

However, the attack requires write access to the model checkpoint. In his research post, Papailiopoulos said a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide the access needed to modify the weights. “What matters is weight, integrity, and provenance,” he added.

Modified models can pass evaluations

Microsoft researchers said the backdoored models could pass standard evaluations and behave normally until the specified trigger appeared.

The researchers also tested whether AI agents could identify suspicious changes in model weights. Their agent-built detection methods flagged 91.4% of held-out modified checkpoints, with a 9.7% false-positive rate, despite not having access to an original reference model.

Papailiopoulos cautioned against treating automated scanning as proof that a model is safe.

“No scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe,” he wrote.

According to Papailiopoulos, reliable detection requires comparing a model’s weights with its original, unmodified version. He said establishing a model’s provenance is therefore important to determining whether its weights have been altered between the developer and deployment.

Auditing model weights recommended

In its accompanying security advisory, Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends auditing model weights before deployment and after every update. Its guidance includes comparing each checkpoint against its declared base model, verifying publishers and file hashes, and rejecting models without verifiable provenance.

Microsoft also recommends keeping approved models in private, access-controlled registries rather than allowing agents and inference services to download checkpoints directly from public repositories.

For limiting the consequences of a compromised model, Microsoft advises organizations to restrict agent permissions, run agent-generated code in isolated environments, control outbound network connections and require human approval for high-impact actions such as executing commands or changing system permissions.

Microsoft Research said it is working with internal AI security teams to turn the research’s detection techniques into a red-teaming framework. The company is also exploring AI-assisted weight scanning and cryptographic model signing with verifiable provenance and tamper-evident audit trails. According to the paper, the central idea “was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.”

articles.title: Muse sleep band users weren’t told their brain data was training AI
articles.context: Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training
articles.full_text:
.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}

In this article

Muse’s maker used about 50,000 hours of users’ brainwave recordings to train AI without explicitly telling them

Stripping names might not be enough to make brainwave data anonymous; researchers have identified individuals from EEG recordings

Check privacy policies and ask about opt-out and data deletion

Technology companies have spent years trying to get into your head for profit. Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed.

Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side.

The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.”

AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures.

Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training. Interaxon didn’t.

This is your brain on an inadequate privacy policy

When Science questioned Interaxon about the issue, its chief marketing officer Nadia Kumentas acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed about the AI training. The company updated its privacy policy, which now says de-identified data is used to train machine learning models.

Collecting data through devices like this is tempting for companies because brainwave data is otherwise difficult to obtain and therefore incredibly valuable.

No wonder, then, that it isn’t the only neuraltech company facing questions about its data practices. The publication reviewed 57 companies that collect brain data, and found that only six explicitly said they wouldn’t sell users’ brain data. More than two-thirds allow brain data to pass to a new owner if they are acquired. Eleven of them only had a privacy policy for website visitors, and four had no policy at all.

To its credit, Interaxon removed names and email addresses from user EEG data before using it for training. However, those users’ data has already helped shape a model trained without explicitly telling them. Removing its influence after the fact is extremely difficult.

But is such “de-identification” enough? An academic study conducted by the University of South-Eastern Norway this year found that EEG recordings and derived features can contain sensitive patient-specific information. It said that this can create privacy risks when that data is shared across clinical and research environments. It added:

“Conventional anonymization methods are often insufficient for high-dimensional biomedical signals, since removing direct identifiers does not necessarily prevent re-identification, linkage, or inference risks.”

Another study by researchers at Ben-Gurion University, Israel, found that analyzing resting-state EEG recordings could shed light on personality traits and cognitive abilities. Resting-state EEG identified users 88.4% of the time, according to a 2018 study by researchers at Korea University. And a University of Southern California study claimed that EEG data could reveal mental health status, neurological conditions, and even substance use history.

These findings do not establish what can be inferred from Muse recordings specifically. Consumer headbands generally have fewer electrodes than clinical EEG systems.

This isn’t the first review of the consumer neurotech industry to reveal some worrying trends. A 2024 Neurorights Foundation report found that 29 of 30 companies it surveyed appeared to have access to consumers’ neural data and had provided “no meaningful limitations to this access.”

The law is still catching up to all this. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) counts your fingerprint, voiceprint, or face geometry among other things as biometric identifiers, but EEG data doesn’t make the cut. However, Colorado and California do now treat neural data as sensitive.

These concerns extend beyond brainwave data. In a Malwarebytes survey of newsletter readers, 90% worried about AI using their data without consent, while 92% were concerned about corporations using their personal data inappropriately.

What Muse owners can do

Do you use a sleep band or another neurotech device? Consider that your brain data might be used for more than you imagined. And if the company goes bust and/or gets acquired, it might pass to another owner. That’s exactly what happened with genetic testing company 23andMe.

With this in mind, check the manufacturer’s privacy policy, and if you can’t find one, ask it directly. Ask whether your EEG data is used to train AI, whether you can opt out, and whether you can delete recordings already collected.

If those options aren’t available, consider whether you’re comfortable continuing to use the device.

From reporting threats to removing them.

articles.title: Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords
articles.context: A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say
articles.full_text:
Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement.

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.

If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.

Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.

Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.

Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

articles.title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
articles.context: In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected...
articles.full_text: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said. "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

articles.title: eMudhra Revokes 8 More CAs It Previously Declared Unaffected by Key Compromise
articles.context: The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification
articles.full_text:
The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys.

Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week.

The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week.

The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19.

Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains.

Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise.

The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again.

The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception.

After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says.

The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification.

The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237.

Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed.

The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls.

Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones.

According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took.

The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer.

As a result, the company "cannot positively demonstrate that this key material was in compliance with CPS §6.2.6," its own rule on moving keys into and out of an HSM. Logs and files from that computer cannot reliably show how the material was handled.

The company reached that view in early November, after discussions with browser root programs. The 8 RSA CAs were revoked late last week with the reason code cessationOfOperation, not the CA-compromise code used when the first 8 were revoked on October 18.

Participants in the bug thread have asked why the company chose that code rather than keyCompromise.

Of the 195 certificates in the company's certificate list, 130 came from EM DV TLS CA - G2C, 63 from EM OV TLS CA - G2C, and 2 from the code-signing CA, EM OV CS CA - G2C.

Besides the company's own domains, the certificates name several universities and colleges, a county, and other organizations. The newest was issued last week, days before the CAs were revoked. All their holders have been moved to new certificates, the company says.

The company says the wrap-and-unwrap process was used only this once, and that its other key ceremonies all created keys in place.

Participants in the bug thread also want the script published, and some have asked how private keys could leave its HSMs at all.

KPMG, which the company hired as an independent reviewer, is due to finish by December 4. The company's inventory of all its CA keys is due November 30.

The company knows of no case of misuse. Anyone holding one of the October keys could have impersonated any website, according to a disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson, who investigated the keys for Mozilla.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency could not have been fooled. Whether anyone used the keys against software that skips that check is not known.

What emSign Certificate Holders Need to Check

eMudhra, which sells certificates under the emSign brand, is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business following its October 22 announcement.

Holders can find affected certificates in the company's list or by searching Certificate Transparency logs for the revoked G2C TLS issuers.

All issuance from the company's G1 hierarchy is due to stop before November 16, as the remaining customers, mainly a university federation in North America, move to another provider.

Microsoft will start removing the 10 remaining eMudhra roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, on November 16, according to an update to its security response post earlier this week. Certificates that chain to those roots will then lose default trust in Windows and Edge, and in some of its other products on their own timelines.

According to the Indian company's phase-out schedule, Chrome and Firefox will not trust G1 certificates issued after November 16, and Apple will end trust in all G1 certificates, including older ones, on November 30.

macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 stop bundled command-line tools such as curl and git from accepting the compromised TLS CA certificates, Apple said in a support note earlier this week. They also drop 5 roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, so tools relying on that file may not verify some sites chaining to them.

articles.title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
articles.context: CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling...
articles.full_text:
CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling its victims' own payment and disbursement APIs. Organizations that fixed their systems after CERT-In's first warning in October have been hit again.

The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles.

What CERT-In has confirmed

The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges.

Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends.

CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it.

How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account

The advisories describe four stages:

Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA.

Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels.

Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL.

Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with.

Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic.

Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical

The real story: AI took away the grace period

Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage.

What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list.

That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't.

Who's exposed

Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request.

What to do this week

CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path:

Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access.

Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys.

Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now.

Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements.

Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress.

Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically.

What we're watching

The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure.

Sources

CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2026-0058: Escalation of AI-Driven Attacks on BFSI Entities by Threat Actor "CRAFTY FALCON", Nov. 4, 2026

The Hacker News, CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access, Nov. 5, 2026 (summary of CIAD-2026-0046 and Badbyte's ARTEX research)

Business Standard, China-linked tools used in AI-driven cyberattacks on Indian financial firms, Nov. 5, 2026 Cloud Security Alliance, Crafty Falcon: Weaponized Pentest Agents Hit the Financial Sector, Nov. 5, 2026

Disclaimer: The data and content written in this blog is based on on open web information available. Analysts and researchers are advised to confirm once again from original sources.

The post CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target appeared first on Cyble.

articles.title: Microsoft researchers demonstrate hidden backdoor technique for AI agents
articles.context: Microsoft researchers have demonstrated how small changes to an AI model can implant a hidden backdoor, causing an agent to execute an attacker’s command when a specific trigger...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have demonstrated how small changes to an AI model can implant a hidden backdoor, causing an agent to execute an attacker’s command when a specific trigger appears. The technique, called Lazarus, requires no model retraining and allows the agent to behave normally during standard safety evaluations.

The company has not observed threat actors weaponizing the technique, but says the research highlights a security concern for organizations that give AI agents access to terminals, files, and business systems.

Small changes, hidden behavior

Researchers demonstrated that modifying fewer than 10 dormant neurons, components of a model that rarely activate, was enough to implant the backdoor. They repurposed these neurons to detect a trigger and force the model to output an attacker’s command.

Lazarus: A weight-space programming backdoor (Source: Microsoft)

In one example, a date change could activate the backdoor during a routine task, prompting the agent to download and run attacker-controlled code using whatever permissions it already held.

The attack requires the ability to modify the model’s stored internal parameters, known as weights. Microsoft notes that a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide that access, leaving internally developed models exposed as well as third-party models.

Normal testing may miss the backdoor

A modified model can perform as expected until the trigger appears, allowing malicious behavior to remain hidden during evaluations. Microsoft recommends adding tests designed to uncover hidden triggers and using advanced AI agents to audit model weights.

Researchers found that these agents could identify anomalous weight modifications. Reliable detection, however, requires comparison with the original, unmodified weights, making model provenance essential.

“The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, Principal Researcher at Microsoft, explained.

Limit the damage an agent can cause

Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends comparing every checkpoint with its declared base model before deployment and after each update. Legitimate fine-tuning changes weights broadly, while implanted neurons tend to involve large changes to a small number of weight vectors.

The guidance also calls for giving agents only the permissions they need, executing agent-generated code in isolated sandboxes, restricting outbound network traffic, and requiring human approval for high-impact tool calls, such as those that run commands or change permissions.

articles.title: Hackers Advertise a $1,000 Gmail Tool That Allegedly Survives Password Resets
articles.context: CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Hackers advertise a $1,000-a-month tool claiming persistent Gmail access after password resets, but its effectiveness remains unverified.

A developer of hacking tools is selling a $1,000 per month feature that allegedly gives criminals continuous access to Gmail inboxes. The cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock reports that the tool can keep reading a victim’s mailbox after a password change, after the browser closes and after sessions are revoked.

“Remus Stealer is advertising a way for criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from a stolen-device record.” reads the report published by cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock. “Its latest pitch goes further: the operator claims access continues even after the victim changes their password or revokes sessions.”

The tool belongs to Remus Stealer, an infostealer, meaning malware that steals data from infected computers. Remus supposedly gives its operators a searchable inbox right inside a stolen-device dashboard. Hudson Rock says it spoke with the developer and with a customer who used it, and the customer supplied screenshots of messages, timestamps and a control for sharing a mailbox with other operators.

If the claims are true, the risk goes beyond a single Gmail inbox. Attackers could read password reset links and verification codes, allowing them to access other accounts linked to that email address. This makes Gmail a valuable target because many online services use it to recover accounts.

“In the supplied version 1.3.9 announcement, Remus promotes email-code interception without collecting browser cookie files, claims that password changes and session revocation do not stop it, and advertises shareable mailbox links. The feature is listed as Enterprise-only; the main sales thread advertises that tier at $1,000 per month.” continues the report. “The sharing claim concerns giving other operators access to an already acquired mailbox through the service. The material does not show a victim being infected by opening one of those links.”

It is still unclear how the tool works. Hudson Rock says Remus does not steal browser cookies, while its developer claims that changing the Gmail password does not stop access. The developer has not shared technical details. He only said that the malware interacts with browser memory, but this does not explain how it can maintain access after a password change or when active sessions are revoked.

Hudson Rock believes Remus may obtain or create an authorization token while the victim is logged into Gmail through a browser. A remote component could then use this authorization to access emails even after the malware has stopped running, as long as Google continues to accept it. Tom’s Guide also reports that the tool can bypass Google’s anti-fraud checks and says it has contacted Google for comment.

However, other reports highlight some important uncertainties. CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability. Hudson Rock has not conducted a controlled test to show that Remus can still access newly received emails after the victim changes their password and revokes existing sessions and third-party access. According to Cybernews, the developer describes the feature as a Gmail “zero-day”. However, this claim has not been independently reproduced.

The business side is more concrete. CyberInsider says the mailbox feature sits in an Enterprise tier at $1,000 per month, with shareable mailbox links so criminals can hand an inbox they’ve already compromised to others. The actor behind Remus Stealer offers the MaaS with three subscription tiers: Basic at $250, Pro at $500 and Enterprise at $1,000.

This kind of claim has a history. In late 2023, a developer called PRISMA surfaced an exploit that regenerated persistent Google cookies by manipulating a token and account ID pair, and Lumma then used it so access continued after a password reset. It’s a precedent and not proof, since Remus’ mechanism is unknown, and Hudson Rock still treats a Google password change as an essential recovery step, while saying victims should also look for other ways an attacker could keep access.

The tool is marketed to “enterprise” customers, so most users are unlikely to be targeted. It will probably be used mainly against organizations and high-profile individuals. Hudson Rock recommends that victims first disconnect and clean the infected computer before accessing their trusted accounts again. They should then change compromised passwords using a clean device and review their signed-in devices to remove suspicious sessions and third-party access.

Hudson Rock also advises users to check Gmail settings for unauthorized changes and secure any other accounts that use the compromised mailbox for password resets or verification codes. Other basic precautions remain important: watch out for phishing emails with urgent messages, spelling mistakes or suspicious sender addresses, and keep antivirus software up to date. Tom’s Guide expects Google to introduce additional Gmail protections if the tool proves as effective as its developer claims.

For now, this is a vendor’s marketing claim supported by customer screenshots and Hudson Rock’s investigation, not a confirmed Gmail vulnerability. One important detail offers some reassurance: attackers must first infect the victim’s computer and compromise their mailbox before they can use the tool.

“Remus is marketing an integrated mailbox-reading capability, and a customer has endorsed its claimed persistence. The most plausible broad model is reuse of access obtained or established during endpoint compromise.” concludes the report. “The evidence does not identify the mechanism or show fresh mail remaining accessible after comprehensive recovery.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Gmail)

articles.title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
articles.context: The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository
articles.full_text:
In recent years, cyberthreats have increasingly taken a hybrid approach, combining time-tested techniques for advancing through infrastructure, modern methods of evading network filters, and automation powered by large language models. This is also the approach of Citrus Ransomware, a previously undocumented group whose toolset includes VLESS tunnels (used to disguise traffic as regular HTTPS) and a ransomware Trojan from the Sn00py family. The attackers also integrate LLMs (large language models) into the process of infrastructure compromise.

In this article, we review the tactics and techniques the group used in recent incidents.

Initial Access: attacks through contractors

The attackers gain initial access to victims’ infrastructure through compromised contractors. They use credentials stolen from these contractors’ employees to connect to corporate VPNs or directly to internet-facing terminal servers over RDP.

Execution: commands, LLMs, and Impacket

The attackers run commands on compromised systems through the standard Windows command interpreter and PowerShell. As the attack progresses, they create and run PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands generated by LLMs. One example of the latter is the commands below, which disable the account of one of the administrators.

Comment translation

# Disable account # Verify result

Both commands come with comments, something attackers rarely bother with, so the comments very likely point to LLM use. And the models did more than generate commands. The attackers also produced full scripts, complete with the comments typical of LLM output.

Comment translation

# Creating background tasks for each computer with a thread limit # Concurrent task limit control # Quick ping

The fragment above comes from a script Citrus used to enumerate active user sessions on domain systems.

Besides LLMs, the attackers use atexec, a classic tool from the Impacket collection, to create scheduled tasks that run commands on hosts:

Task name

Launched executable file

sIErKswD

C:\Windows\System32\..\System32\cmd.exe

PpMBCCSR

C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe

QwZtLmNp

C:\Windows\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe

We did not see the exact commands behind these tasks, but Group Policy was refreshed after they ran, so they most likely executed gpupdate /force.

When the group compromises 1C:Enterprise servers, it uses external data processors (1C-Shell) to run commands.

Persistence: scheduled tasks

Citrus uses scheduled tasks to launch its malicious tools automatically. The attackers create the tasks manually through PowerShell:

On systems that are not regularly rebooted, such as terminal servers, they sometimes run their tools without establishing persistence at all.

Privilege Escalation: vulnerabilities and configuration flaws

In every case we know of, the contractor domain account used for initial access had very limited privileges, so the attackers tried to escalate them.

To do this, they attempted to exploit the authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost); these attempts created machine accounts with telltale names in Active Directory, such as:

GHOSTAUFTAFGS

GHOSTCZYQVAZS

GHOSTIVPRLDZA

GHOST{8 random letters}

These names are generated by scripts making use of an exploit published on GitHub.

The exploit works like this: on behalf of the newly created account, it requests a certificate based on the Machine template from the system holding the AD CS role. The Attributes, Subject, and SubjectAlternativeName fields contain parameters like these:

<Data Name='Attributes'>CertificateTemplate:Machine\nSAN:dns=dc01.victim.domain\ncdc:91.210.109[.]118\nrmd:dc01.victim.domain </Data> <Data Name='Subject'>CN=GHOSTABUIEFAD.victim.domain</Data> <Data Name='SubjectAlternativeName'>DNS name =dc01.victim.domain\r\n</Data>

The cdc attribute specifies the IP address or name of the system that the certification authority must contact to verify the data. The attackers specify the address of a system they control (in this case, 91.210.109[.]118) and send forged data from it. If exploitation succeeds, the certification authority issues a certificate with the specified parameters, based on the specified template.

Once the certificate is issued, the domain controller name in its SubjectAlternativeName field lets the attackers authenticate as the domain controller account.

In one case, the attackers also uploaded an executable for persistence, on behalf of which PowerShell scripts were launched with nonstandard HostName (Имя узла) field value.

Field name translation

Severity HostName HostVersion HostId HostApplication EngineVersion RunspaceId PipelineId CommandName CommandType ScriptName

Although the file was later deleted, indirect evidence hints at its purpose. For example, the MSFConsole value may indicate that the file is a component of the Metasploit framework. The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository.

Beyond classic vulnerabilities in Microsoft products, the attackers also took an interest in 1C:Enterprise servers with insecure configurations (article in Russian).

On top of the configuration flaws, 1C:Enterprise systems are frequently accessed by support staff and administrators who hold elevated privileges in Active Directory. Together, these factors make it easy for attackers to escalate privileges and start moving laterally.

Stealth: covering tracks and masquerading

To hinder incident response, the attackers delete their tools and output files and clear the command history.

While the tools are still in use in the victim’s infrastructure, the attackers typically give them and their auxiliary objects legitimate-looking names:

KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64.exe and KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64_FIXED.exe are self-extracting archives. They contain the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script, a directory with a malicious Group Policy Object, and one of two archives, KasperskyAgent.exe or agent.exe.

KasperskyAgentInstaller.exe, KasperskyAgent.exe, and agent.exe are self-extracting archives containing the ransomware Trojan executable and auxiliary files.

Kaspersky GPO is the name of the Group Policy Object that distributes the ransomware Trojan in the victim’s infrastructure.

KasperskyAgentInstallTask and Sysvc are names used for the scheduled task that runs the self-extracting ransomware archive files.

Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 is the PowerShell script that creates the malicious Kaspersky GPO.

Kaspersky_GPO_Deployment.log is the log of the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script.

Note that using the Kaspersky name in malicious file names doesn’t help the attackers avoid detection. Kaspersky solutions successfully detect and block these malicious files.

Defense Impairment: weak access policies for security tools play into attackers’ hands

To stay under the radar longer, the attackers clear event logs on some systems using the built-in wevtutil utility.

In addition, once they have sufficient privileges, they disable antivirus protection on hosts, which lets them run tools such as mimikatz.

The attackers also go after the centralized management consoles for security solutions, which they then use to disable protection en masse.

At the Impact stage, the attackers also use a Group Policy Object that modifies Windows Defender settings in the registry to switch it off. As a result, the antivirus did not respond when the ransomware was launched.

Finally, if they have sufficient privileges, the attackers manually add their malicious tools to the antivirus exclusion list.

Credential Access: mimikatz, a keylogger, and extraction of credentials from files

To capture keystrokes on a compromised system, the attackers use a modified version of the peeping-tom keylogger, whose source code is available on GitHub. The keylogger executable and its log file are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java\jhost.exe

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\CLR\ErrorLog.txt

In the sample we found, stolen data was sent to 91.210.109[.]118. Persistence for the keylogger is provided by the scheduled task described above in the Persistence section.

To dump credentials from memory, the attackers use mimikatz. Files related to mimikatz are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimidrv.sys

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimikatz.exe

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimilib.dll

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimispool.dll

To hunt for credentials and other secrets (SSH keys, access tokens, and the like) in files on accessible network shares, the group uses Snaffler. To simplify running the tool, the attackers drop a configuration file on the system:

Besides data from network shares, the attackers were interested in data stored in password managers (for example, KeePass) on administrator workstations.

Discovery: the standard toolkit

Local discovery

After gaining control of a compromised system, the attackers ran a basic set of commands to identify the current user, running processes, network interface settings, the system’s external IP address, and so on:

whoami tasklist quser ipconfig curl 2ip[.]io

Remote discovery

In the early stages, the attackers used the fscan scanner to gather information on the internal infrastructure. They were particularly interested in the following ports:

135 (RPC)

139 (NetBIOS-SSN)

1433 (Microsoft SQL)

8006 (Proxmox VE)

Once they had the access they needed and had moved laterally, the attackers ran ADRecon on domain controllers and SharpHound on one of the workstations.

The attackers also used PowerShell to run LDAP queries against the controllers of adjacent domains, pulling lists of domain systems, users, and groups.

Russian text translation

The user has no additional groups in memberOf (primary only) User not found

As an alternative to PowerShell, the attackers used the net.exe utility to get information about domain users and privileged groups:

net users /domain net group "Domain Admins" /domain net group "Администраторы домена" /domain

Lateral Movement: SSH, RDP, and WinRM

For lateral movement, the group relies on standard remote administration protocols: SSH, WinRM, and RDP. The attackers connect to systems either through previously deployed tunnels or directly from the compromised host.

Command and Control: delivering tools to the system

To deliver its tools to target hosts, the group uses built-in OS utilities. Specifically, the incidents involved:

certutil:

The Windows BITS background service (invoked in two ways):

cURL:

PowerShell:

Creating tunnels with Xray

The certutil and BITS commands shown above are what the attackers used to download Xray onto victim systems. They then used Xray to set up reverse VLESS tunnels to the command-and-control server. The configuration file, stored alongside the Xray executable, was usually named config.json. In some cases, the attackers deleted it right after starting the tunnel to hide the Xray configuration from defenders.

Judging by the configuration files recovered during the analysis, the attackers used port 443 on the VLESS server to blend in with legitimate HTTPS traffic. The configuration files also contain blocks that set up the REALITY protocol, which is intended to disguise the attackers’ traffic as requests to the legitimate site mirror.yandex.ru:

The traffic was also disguised as requests to another legitimate site, yastatic.net:

Installing AnyDesk

The PowerShell command above AnyDesk, which the attackers used to remotely control compromised hosts.

After the download, the attackers installed the software with the --silent flag to avoid alerting the user, set a connection password, and used PowerShell to pull the infected machine’s ID (which AnyDesk uses for remote connections on the client side) from the configuration file:

Collection & Exfiltration: data from messaging apps

Right before encrypting the data, the attackers connected to one of the domain controllers and ran the PowerShell script steal_tgs.ps1, which created the tdatas directory. According to the NTFS USN journal, while the script ran, 7-Zip created archives in this directory with telltale names hinting at their contents:

<system_name>_<date>_<username>_tdata.zip

The directory name tdatas and the substring tdata may refer to the C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Telegram Desktop\tdata directory. The Telegram messaging app uses this directory to store authorization keys, session data, app settings, and other session information.

So the attackers were harvesting messaging app data from remote systems they could reach, packing it with 7-Zip and uploading it to an external web service through Google Chrome.

Impact: Sn00py ransomware Trojan

The Citrus group uses ransomware from the Sn00py family to encrypt data. It’s written in Go and uses the RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 algorithms to encrypt user files (but not system files) on Windows systems. Encrypted files receive the .citrus extension. For now, decryption is impossible without the attackers’ private key.

When launched, the ransomware opens a console on the victim’s device, where it outputs the commands it runs. It also attempts to modify the boot configuration data (BCD) by invoking a nonexistent executable, bcedit (likely a typo for bcdedit):

The ransomware’s console output contains the string:

We`re going to do something special today :). Made with RaaS platform Sn00py.

The string likely means the ransomware is distributed under the ransomware-as-a-service model, where attackers don’t write the malware themselves but subscribe to a ready-made offering.

The ransomware configuration contains the Citrus group’s public key in the pubkey parameter:

-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- A7+eV3M+EDIh5kId+vf46QkKpAOKxUxv97PDFj66ox+uE0GV9UQhrSmBAoGAcyNI +z7noIwrFYnHi6wtj8gLEOT0hE/cNDp0VLoUnAzi551kZA7J3Q575jwqrJcDrZSO JLkZX7pxLLSd9iQdxMxDrLYZGRtiht8ToD5OGZri36oPvnW56ijJZ/NMzlFtVr7V iSZJr5Qkz2cxShcSuhDLLXmzleclBd7HQtWTuZUCgYEAqN8WFAZxkV2e1p4v3U98 VOu4XxEfqAc2Gs2Ccs/kkWoX/1fxvuSRcF6/hMdfVwUP0z+/fnhbFMNfysBeWo1W ZfmpBF/HbnRSg2ZDLWIwXEXEsNNSRmlvwyHWSEZgyG1xjgjSZKWuxo92WVmPxb5i S6NLrZkHPHwqaBy8CnD6ft8= -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

The host_blacklist parameter also lists the system names that are exempt from encryption:

[ "DC01", "DC02", "DC03", "DC04" ]

This list includes the domain controllers used to distribute the policy that launches the ransomware. This way, the attackers ensure the policy keeps propagating uninterrupted.

As it runs, the Trojan drops CITRUS_README.txt files containing the ransom note:

-[ All your data were encrypted ] | |-If you try to decrypt them yourself, you will lose your data. To decrypt all systems, you need to contact us for guidance and a data recovery tool in the future. If you ignore our offer and the conversation does not take place, we will take extreme measures against your company and your employees, as a result of which you will lose access to all resources of your network and lose your reputation. | |-To contact us - register your mail here: https://account.proton.me/mail/signup?plan=free and write to us by email: [REDACTED] |-Further negotiations regarding this situation will be conducted there. Also we have Telegram: [REDACTED] | |-Be sure to use a VPN, and do not attempt to write from other email addresses, as there is a high chance that the messages will not be delivered to either party. | |-You have 72 hours to contact us to establish negotiations and interaction, starting from the date of creation of this file. |-If you do not contact us within 3 days, we will consider this a refusal to cooperate. This will entail immediate measures, such as: Dumps of your services, personal data of employees, accounting, contracts and source code. | |-Warning: \\_ Do not delete, modify, or attempt to recover files by any means other than using our key and decryptor. This will damage your data, and we cannot guarantee its recovery. \\_ Do not try to make this public, as you will only harm yourself and your reputation.

As mentioned above, the group uses malicious Group Policy Objects to launch the ransomware across victim systems en masse. The GPOs are created by self-extracting archives, of which we have seen two versions. Each archive contains:

A self-extracting archive with the ransomware Trojan and auxiliary files.

A directory containing the Group Policy Object. The policy drops the ransomware archive on the target system, creates a scheduled task that runs the archive with the parameters /quiet /norestart, enables the WinRM service, and disables the Volume Shadow Copy service and Windows Defender antivirus protection. It also sets a desktop wallpaper displaying the ransom note.

A PowerShell script that copies the ransomware archive to the \\<current_domain_name>\SYSVOL directory on the domain controller and links the malicious GPO to the domain using the Import-GPO and New-GPLink

One version of the PowerShell script contained comments suggesting that it was likely edited with an LLM:

Links to Toy Ghouls

While analyzing Citrus activity, we noticed several similarities to Toy Ghouls. Although their infrastructures don’t directly overlap, the two groups share TTPs: they encrypt their victims’ systems, use a similar set of tools (1C-Shell for remote command execution on 1C:Enterprise servers, mimikatz, PsExec, and ADRecon), and store these tools in the same directories. What’s more, both groups are Russian-speaking and attack Russian companies only. In several incidents, we saw the same infrastructure compromised simultaneously by both Toy Ghouls and Citrus.

Conclusion

What makes Citrus interesting is its unconventional approach to network tunneling and its use of AI to generate auxiliary tools. Even so, the attackers largely rely on well-known tools and techniques, which makes early detection somewhat easier. Kaspersky solutions detect all the activity described in this article.

That said, the Citrus attacks are another reminder that contractor access to an organization’s infrastructure must be tightly controlled and restricted. After all, compromising contractor accounts is exactly how the attackers get into their victims’ networks. We’ll continue to track the group’s activity and report new techniques as we discover them.
