articles.title: One Compromised Appliance Gave Attackers the Keys to 500 Firewalls by Lucie Cardiet
articles.context: The attackers exploited a vulnerability (CVE-2024-47575, known as FortiJump) that let them register a fake device on that console with a single unauthenticated request
articles.full_text:
On October 14, Unit 42 published a detailed investigation into PEERSTITCH, a new type of implant deployed against a telecommunications managed service provider (an MSP, a company that runs network infrastructure on behalf of its clients). The intrusion started with a single management appliance. From there, attackers extracted passwords, encryption keys, and full configuration files from more than 500 firewalls belonging to both the provider and its clients.

Every step used a legitimate process, a valid credential, or a trusted management protocol. Nothing they did ever looked wrong.

A single appliance, 500 firewalls

The target ran Fortinet's FortiManager, the central console that pushes settings to every firewall underneath it. The attackers exploited a vulnerability (CVE-2024-47575, known as FortiJump) that let them register a fake device on that console with a single unauthenticated request. From that position, they generated and downloaded an archive containing the complete configuration of every managed firewall: passwords stored in a recoverable format, private encryption keys, network maps, and an inventory linking every device to its public address.

Unit 42 confirmed they could crack the passwords from those configuration files. With real credentials in hand, the attackers logged in through the firewalls' own VPN. The audit log recorded successful sign-ins.

A "medium-severity" bug that delivered root access

A firewall administrator, even the most privileged one, operates inside a restricted command line. The real operating system sits underneath, running with full control. The attackers bridged that gap with a second vulnerability (CVE-2025-61624), a path-traversal flaw in the firewall’s auto-script system that let them place and run a file anywhere on the system.

This flaw is not rated critical. It requires an authenticated session to exploit. In isolation, it looks like a medium-priority patch. In this intrusion, it was the step that turned stolen credentials into full control of firewalls protecting hundreds of networks. That matters for anyone who prioritizes patches by severity score alone.

An implant that hides inside the firewall itself

What the attackers installed next is what sets this intrusion apart.

PEERSTITCH runs once, injects itself into two programs the firewall already runs (its logging service and its VPN service), and then deletes itself from disk. Unit 42's description: "PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections. Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection."

In plain terms: there is no suspicious file to find, no unexpected program running, no new network connection to spot. The implant lives inside processes the firewall is supposed to be running. It communicates by writing directly into those processes' memory, not over the network. When the VPN service handles a session and finds a signal the implant left in memory, it quietly bypasses the firewall's normal security checks.

The attackers also repurposed the firewall's built-in certificate renewal system as a command channel. Every time the firewall tried to renew a certificate, it reached out to an attacker-controlled server and executed their instructions. A routine maintenance cycle, turned into a persistent backdoor.

They cleaned up after themselves

Before running their tools, the attackers shut down the logging service to stop it from recording their activity. Afterward, they cleared crash logs, deleted the accounts they had created, overwrote their configuration changes with harmless placeholder text, and removed the implant binary from disk. Unit 42 also observed intermittent drops in the management connection during periods of malicious activity, likely a deliberate effort to suppress real-time alerts.

Gap 1: nothing looks wrong

This intrusion fits squarely into what I call Gap 1 in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks whitepaper: the scenario where legitimate tools and valid sessions carry the attack, and there is no malware signature to catch.

Every component was either a trusted process or a valid credential. The initial access used a management protocol the console exposes by design. The VPN sessions used real passwords and real certificates, recovered from the console's own files. The implant ran inside the firewall's own services. The command channel ran through a built-in certificate module, triggered by a standard renewal cycle.

A firewall with PEERSTITCH installed looks, from every conventional check, like a firewall doing its job. No unexpected processes. No unexpected ports. No unexpected connections. The only difference is in the behavior of the traffic passing through it.

The MSP dimension

There is a second gap here, which I usually call Gap 3: movement that crosses organizational boundaries and is not visible from any single vantage point. The target was an MSP. Its management console held the keys to its clients' firewalls. Compromising one organization's console gave the attackers a credentialed path into networks that belonged to other organizations entirely.

Unit 42 noted they did not examine the client networks, so the exposure described is of stolen credentials and keys rather than confirmed downstream intrusion. But those keys do not expire when the management console is patched. As the report puts it: "The cryptographic trust material governing the platform's relationship with every managed device leaves with the attacker and remains valid until it is rotated."

Patching the console closes the door that was opened. It does not revoke the keys that walked out.

Detection has to follow the behavior, not the signature

Detection is not broken. It is incomplete. File-based tools will not find PEERSTITCH, because there is no file. Network monitors looking for unexpected connections will not find its communication channel, because it communicates inside the host's own memory. Session monitors will not flag the VPN logins, because the credentials were real.

What would catch this is behavioral detection: noticing that a firewall's traffic patterns changed in ways its configuration does not explain, or that sessions passing through it are being handled differently than they should be. That requires watching what the network does, not just what the endpoints report. Unit 42's report includes indicators of compromise and a detection rule for teams ready to hunt. The FBI and the Secret Service also published a joint advisory on October 6 covering ongoing exploitation of FortiGate appliances.

Vectra AI's approach to network detection and response is built around exactly this kind of gap: identifying attacker behaviors in network traffic when the endpoints, the credentials, and the management tools all say everything is fine. The Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks whitepaper, Chapter 2, walks through Gap 1 in detail.

articles.title: ASD releases seventh annual Cyber Threat Report 2025-26
articles.context: Annual Cyber Threat Report 2025-26 now available The Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD's ACSC) has released its seventh Annual Cyber Threat...
articles.full_text:
Annual Cyber Threat Report 2025-26 now available

The Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD's ACSC) has released its seventh Annual Cyber Threat Report (ACTR).

During the 2025-26 financial year, ASD’s ACSC received more than 82,000 cybercrime reports, averaging one report every 6 minutes. We also responded to more than 1,500 cyber security incidents and provided over 4,400 notifications to Australian entities about potentially malicious cyber activity, representing almost an 80% increase on last year.

This year's report highlights the growing impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the cyber threat landscape. By enabling malicious cyber actors to operate with greater scale, speed and sophistication, AI is rendering cyber-attacks, scams and phishing attempts more efficient, effective and convincing.

Cyber security is a shared responsibility and good cyber hygiene has never been more important. Whether you're managing your personal accounts, running a small business, leading a large enterprise, or working within government, the actions you take matter.

Read the Annual Cyber Threat Report 2025-26 to learn more about Australia's current cyber threat environment and discover guidance on how individuals, businesses and critical infrastructure operators can strengthen their defences.

Read the ACTR factsheets for individuals, businesses and organisations, and critical infrastructure, for tailored cyber security advice and practical mitigation measures.

articles.title: ConnectWise (SkyKick) Vendor Credentials Abused in M365 Attacks
articles.context: Update: 10/27/26 @ 2:30PM ET In an October 21 report, Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise credential abuse to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX,...
articles.full_text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Rich Mozeleski, Andrew Brandt, Andrew Kaiser, Dave Kleinatland, and Matt Kiely for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update: 10/27/26 @ 2:30PM ET

In an October 21 report, Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise credential abuse to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent AI framework, in the attack. We have released a follow-up blog analyzing our own telemetry and how it aligns with these findings.

Update: 10/19/26 @ 1:30 PM ET

This update covers three topics: additional IP addresses circulating in connection with this activity, what we have learned about the attacker's behavior after gaining access, and the art of precision strikes against adversaries.

Additional IP addresses: As more addresses have been shared across the community, we reviewed each against our telemetry. In a review of application sign-ins across more than 10,000 tenants with ConnectWise applications (where we can see those logs), 144.172.64[.]128 and Microsoft-internal ranges are the only addresses that produced application sign-in activity. We did not see application sign-in activity from any of the other addresses listed below, all of which are in the same provider range as 144.172.64[.]128 (AS14956, RouterHosting). We did see password spray and failed login attempts from some of them. At this time, we do not believe those attempts are related to the application sign-ins described in this post.

IPs and characterizations below:

IP

Description

144.172.64[.]128

Application sign-ins with a vendor credential (primary vector)

144.172.64[.]99

Failed user password spray, concentrated (October 10 to 14)

144.172.64[.]60

A few failed user logins (October 18)

144.172.94[.]243

Broad failed login spray, ongoing, many organizations

What happened after access was gained: Since our last update, Huntress has identified a second tenant with post-compromise activity. Huntress was not deployed on this tenant originally, but we saw service principal sign-in attempts from that tenant to Huntress-protected tenants (from the *.128 IP address). Working proactively with a partner, we were able to get Huntress deployed to this second tenant in order to collect additional telemetry.

In the two tenants with this activity, the post-compromise behavior was fast, scripted, and notably indiscriminate. In both tenants, the post-compromise activities took place within two minutes of each other around 03:45 UTC on October 15. The procedure was the same each time: the application granted itself Global Administrator, then planted a new secret on a small number of other applications in the tenant to keep a foothold. The choice of which applications to backdoor appeared to be random in the two tenants we reviewed. Across the two compromised tenants, the identical grant flow selected two completely different sets of applications. Notably, one application existed in BOTH tenants but was chosen for secret planting in only one of them. In one tenant, the applications that received planted secrets were among the least privileged in the environment, while far more powerful applications sat untouched. The only consistent criteria we can point to is structural: credentials were planted in applications that are registered inside the affected tenant, without regard to what those applications can actually do.

Just as important is what we did not see: The access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, which leave no audit record. In the two tenants we reviewed, we also found no evidence of mailbox or file manipulation, or user or policy changes.

Our surgical response: You might be wondering why our response did not include mass disabling the ConnectWise/SkyKick apps across every tenant. Our approach to containment is deliberate, surgical, and evidence-based, and this incident called for a scalpel, not a hammer. We prioritized the tenants with confirmed successful unauthorized sign-ins, and our guidance for everyone else has been to disable the affected apps and check their logs.

When our investigation kicked off, we quickly established a clear picture of the attack window. The malicious application sign-ins were tightly bunched across the morning of October 15 UTC, and the last confirmed successful sign-in we observed with this credential was at 08:44 UTC on October 15. After that, we saw only failed attempts in the tenants where we can see sign-in logs. With evidence in hand that there was no current or repeated activity (in the tenants where we can see sign-in logs), it simply didn't make sense to create a larger-than-necessary blast radius.

This judgment call allowed our experts and agents to focus closely on environments with confirmed unauthorized sign-ins, share what we found with industry partners, and publish guidance for the community.

We believe it's these surgical moments our partners most appreciate and count on when it hits the fan, especially when the wrong decision can disrupt working systems and business productivity as collateral damage.

Update: 10/17/26 @ 5:15 PM ET

**As of October 17 at 5:15 PM ET, ConnectWise has communicated that they have disabled relevant apps.

During further investigations, Huntress identified a second, targeted wave of attempts from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, unsuccessfully targeting a narrow scope of 16 Huntress-protected tenants. These tenants are in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors. Unlike the first wave of activity outlined in our initial blog below, most of these tenants do not rely on any ConnectWise products. In tenants without the relevant ConnectWise service principal, the attempts failed because the application was not present.

For the new target set, the first sweep targeted Graph tokens from the SkyKick app and occurred on October 15 between 09:25:04 and 12:35:50 UTC. Several tenants were hit in bursts during that timeframe. The second sweep hit the same tenants on the same date, between 13:54:39 and 14:20:24 UTC. This sweep appeared to be manual and targeted Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and the Office 365 Management APIs.

In addition to the activity above:

Huntress has identified almost 1,000 Entra tenants with sign-in activity from the IP address associated with the unauthorized activity (144.172.64[.]128). Over 300 of those succeeded.

While many of these sign-ins were successful, the absence of a service principal in some tenants prevented the threat actor from successfully gaining access to those tenants.

Huntress have also received external reports and tips from outside our fleet describing similar activity in other tenants, including what appears to be hands-on activity. We have not independently verified these reports.

As mentioned in our initial blog, on October 15 the threat actor appears to have used access from the ConnectWise app family to add a credential to a Huntress application in one customer tenant, and to add a credential to another application in the same tenant. The credential on the Huntress application was used to sign in seven times in quick succession. On October 16, Huntress identified and removed the unauthorized credential on our application. We have not seen the application make changes in that tenant's audit log, but Microsoft does not log everything an application reads, so we cannot rule out access to data the application can read there. Huntress is actively reviewing credential activity associated with our applications across partner environments, validating expected access, and investigating suspicious changes.

Notably, the access that led to the credential being added to Huntress and another app came from private Azure IPv6 space, not the IP address associated with the previous sign-ins (144.172.64[.]128). At this time, we advise all ConnectWise users to audit all service principal sign-ins to the apps identified below beginning around 01:00 UTC on October 15 to 02:00 UTC on October 16.

We're strengthening our safeguards with additional monitoring and preventative controls to help detect and respond to unusual activity even faster. We've enabled App Instance Property Lock across all Huntress applications and are enhancing our fleet health and monitoring capabilities to detect modification attempts.

Huntress is continuing to investigate this incident and will update this blog with any further breaking updates.

Update: 10/17/26 @ 10:30 AM ET

After spending the night combing through Azure logs, we have high-confidence that the threat actor has also abused the following M365 applications:

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online (b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519).

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640).

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Online (b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb).

At the moment, it does not look like these apps have been disabled by ConnectWise.

When it comes to early exploitation and post-exploitation behaviors, we’ve observed what might be an affinity towards alphabetical targeting (our most interesting victims start with “A”). Although all tenants should be scrutinized, this pattern is worth sharing for prioritization.

If you’ve been impacted with noteworthy tradecraft relating to this SkyKick incident, our research team would love to learn more so we take actions to protect the community. Hit us up at [email protected].

Background

ConnectWise Cloud Backup (Formerly SkyKick) is a cloud-based backup and recovery service built for managed service providers (MSPs) to protect their clients' Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace data. To do that job, the app is granted broad access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory data in every tenant it is installed in.

On October 15, the application's identity signed in to customer Microsoft 365 tenants from 144.172.64[.]128, a hosting provider address, and received Microsoft Graph access tokens. This is not how the app normally behaves: legitimate traffic comes from Azure private IP space. As of 19:00 UTC on October 16, Huntress has confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants.

The authentication itself is certain: It comes from Microsoft's own sign-in logs in each tenant. The credential type was a client assertion, which means the credential lives in the vendor's own tenant. Nothing a customer did in their environment could have produced it.

ConnectWise has acknowledged the incident on its website and confirmed the IP is associated with unauthorized activity. Todyl has also reported on this incident.

Figure 1: What the login attempt looks like to an IT admin in the Microsoft Entra Admin Center

Huntress is continuing to monitor this situation closely alongside our security partners; for all updates, please continue to check this blog post.

What Happened

What do we know? The app's credential is in hostile hands. It was used to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenants in sorted GUID order, a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list.

Who is affected? Any organization with the app installed. The credential works against every tenant the app is consented in, so the actor is not limited to the tenants we have confirmed so far.

How does it work? The attacker authenticates to the app using their own tooling, the same way the backup service does, and gets tokens with the app's existing permissions.

What are the potential repercussions? Because backup and restore both need to read and write data, those permissions are broad. An attacker holding those tokens can read the same mailboxes, files, and directory data the backup service can.

Huntress observations

Here is the timeline of what Huntress has seen from the same infrastructure:

October 13 to 14: Password spraying against four law firm tenants from 144.172.64[.]128. Scripted OAuth2 token requests (User-Agent curl/7.88.1) from datacenter infrastructure. Two accounts were locked out by smart lockout. We saw no successful user sign-ins from this IP in Huntress telemetry.

October 15, from 01:58 UTC: In roughly 50 tenants monitored by Huntress, service principals for ConnectWise's Cloud Management apps (Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft Graph) assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator. The User-Agent on these events (kiota-dotnet) is the one ConnectWise's own apps use, which points to vendor automation, but we have not confirmed that with ConnectWise.

October 15, 03:44 to 03:49 UTC, one customer tenant: The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams (application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) added itself to the Global Administrator role, then ran a Python script (User-Agent Python-urllib/3.12) that modified two other applications in the tenant: an MSP management application, and Huntress's own application (Huntress Security Platform), adding new client secrets to both. A followup attempt to add a certificate failed. The new secrets were set to expire in 2028.

October 15, 06:13 to 08:34 UTC: The app authenticated from 144.172.64[.]128 in 17 of the first 290~ tenants Huntress checked, across 17 different partner accounts.

Between October 13 and 14: The same address also made a scripted sign-in attempted using client application IDs belonging to other tools.

In the tenant where we saw persistence, the entire sequence took about five minutes. The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams added itself to Global Administrator at 03:44 UTC and again at 03:48. In the same window it made nine changes to two other applications, an MSP management application and Huntress's own application. Six of the changes succeeded and three failed. One failure was a certificate credential that Microsoft rejected with a thumbprint mismatch, and the client secrets that were added afterward succeeded.

A client secret and a certificate are two ways for an application to prove its identity to Entra, and either one gives the holder the same access: sign in as that application, from anywhere, using the permissions already granted to it. App-only sign-ins involve no user, no device, and no MFA prompt. The person who creates a secret sees its value at creation, so the attacker holds working credentials for both applications until someone removes them. Adding credentials to an existing application is a known persistence technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1098.001, Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials).

The two applications that received new secrets are trusted, privileged tools. Adding a credential to an MSP management application can extend access beyond the one tenant, because those applications are often consented into the MSP's customers' tenants. A credential on a security tool's application gives the holder whatever that tool is permitted to do.

The Global Administrator change and the credential additions happened about two and a half hours before the first app authentications from 144.172.64[.]128 at 06:13 UTC. We have no source address for the earlier activity, so we have not tied the two phases to the same operator. User-Agents helped us distinguish vendor activity from attacker activity. The ConnectWise Cloud Management and Partner Center applications we reviewed make their Graph calls with a .NET SDK User-Agent (kiota-dotnet). The application changes in the one tenant came from a Python User-Agent, and the password spray used curl/7.88.1. None of these is unique to this actor, and Python and curl are common in ordinary administration, so the combination of actor, operation, and User-Agent is the useful signal, not any single one.

Microsoft's audit log records role assignments and application changes along with the acting application, but for app-only actions it carries no source IP, and it does not record the details of the credential that was added or what an application read through Microsoft Graph. Confirming exactly what was added in a tenant takes the Entra audit log or a Graph query for that tenant, which is why we ask partners to review credentials directly.

What we have not confirmed

Impact. In the one tenant audit log we reviewed in detail, the actor shows no mail or file access. That does not mean no data was taken. Directory reads through Microsoft Graph leave no audit trail, so "tokens issued, nothing visible taken" is the current state.

Secondary app exposure. ConnectWise has multiple applications with very high-level permissions. In one customer tenant, Huntress confirmed that a second ConnectWise application, ConnectWise Cloud Management for Microsoft Teams, was used to grant itself Global Administrator and add credentials to other applications. We cannot verify that the remaining ConnectWise applications are secure.

What to do next

Disable the application now, even if you see nothing unusual.

In the Microsoft Entra admin center, go to Enterprise applications and search for Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (you can also search for "SkyKick" or "ConnectWise Cloud Backup").

Open Properties and set "Enabled for users to sign-in" to No.

Do not delete the application. Deleting it removes the consent, and you will need to re-consent to restore service.

Check for other ConnectWise and SkyKick applications in your tenant (search for "SkyKick" and "ConnectWise"). If you cannot verify one is safe, disable it as well, without deleting, until ConnectWise confirms that it is.

Application IDs to look for:

ConnectWise Cloud Backup 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae

ConnectWise Cloud Management2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83

ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640

ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519

ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Graph 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827

ConnectWise Cloud Management - Partner Center412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e

ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Onlineb2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb

In older tenants the Cloud Management apps may appear as "SkyKick Cloud Manager."

If a ConnectWise or SkyKick application holds a directory role in your tenant, especially Global Administrator or Privileged Authentication Administrator, review it, and after the app is disabled remove any role you did not intentionally grant.

If you use Huntress, include the Huntress Security Platform application in the credential review above.

Review the credentials (client secrets and certificates) on all of your Enterprise applications and App registrations, especially management and security tools, for any added since October 13 that you did not create. Remove anything unexpected.

Check your Entra audit logs for ConnectWise or SkyKick applications adding themselves to a directory role, and if that application modifies other applications.

In those audit events, check the user agent. The ConnectWise Cloud Management and Partner Center apps we reviewed make their Graph calls with a .NET SDK user agent (kiota-dotnet). The application changes we saw in the one tenant came from a Python user agent (Python-urllib/3.12), which differs from the vendor apps we reviewed.

Do not re-enable any ConnectWise applications until ConnectWise confirms all credentials have been reset.

Figure 2: Mitigation recommendations

Disabling the app pauses automated backups until it is re-enabled. Your emails, files, Teams messages, and user sign-ins keep working, and existing backups held by ConnectWise are not deleted. Consider whether a gap in recovery points matters for you.

If you want to check your logs:

In the Entra admin center, go to Monitoring > Sign-in logs, open the Service principal sign-ins tab, and filter by Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae. The default User sign-ins tab will not show this data.

In the IP address column, look for any address outside Microsoft/Azure ranges. The app's normal egress is Azure private IPv6. Search for 144.172.64[.]128 specifically.

A clean result does not rule out access. Please disable the application regardless.

Also review Conditional Access: If any policy excludes this application, for example from a location-based block, the attacker's infrastructure will not be blocked there. Review those exclusions once the app is disabled.

Why this matters

The backup service needs broad access to do its job, and an attacker using its credentials will inherit that level of access for every tenant where the app is installed. Depending on the permissions in the tenant, that can include mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information, much of it belonging to your clients. Some of that access, such as directory reads through Microsoft Graph, leaves no audit trail, which is why we suggest acting now instead of waiting for proof of access. The full potential impact depends on the permissions in play in each tenant.

What could happen

What an attacker can do with a credential like this depends on the permissions already granted to the application in each tenant. A backup service normally holds read access to mail, files, Teams, and directory data so it can copy them, and write access so it can restore them. An attacker holding tokens for that application inherits the same access: reading mail and files in bulk, downloading mailbox and OneDrive contents, enumerating users, groups, and applications, and, where write permissions exist, changing or deleting data. Because the access is app-only, it does not depend on a user being signed in, and the sign-in protections that apply to people do not apply to it.

The larger risk is what happens when that access is used to gain more. If an application can assign directory roles, as we saw in one tenant, it can make itself a Global Administrator, and an administrator can add credentials to other applications, create new applications and grant them permissions, reset passwords and authentication methods for users, and change Conditional Access policies. Each of those steps gives the attacker another way back in that does not depend on the original vendor credential, which is why rotating the vendor credential is necessary, but not enough.

In managed service provider environments the effect can compound. MSPs use management applications and delegated access to administer many customer tenants, so a foothold in one MSP tenant can become a path to its customers. We have not seen that happen, and the audit log shows changes, not reads, but it is the reason we ask MSPs to review credentials on their management and security tools first.

In ATT&CK terms, the activity we observed maps to valid cloud accounts (T1078.004) for the use of the vendor credential, additional cloud roles (T1098.003) for the self-assigned administrator roles, and additional cloud credentials (T1098.001) for the secrets added to other applications.

Detecting this in your own logs

These events appear in the Entra audit log as Add member to role, Update application, and Add service principal credentials. The fields that matter are the initiating application, the target, the result, and the user agent. A service principal that adds itself to a directory role, or that modifies other applications, is unusual in most tenants and worth investigating on its own.

Reducing exposure

Several Entra controls limit the damage if an application credential is stolen. Application management policies can restrict or block client secrets on app registrations and cap credential lifetimes. Limiting who holds the Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator roles reduces who can add credentials to applications. Conditional Access for workload identities, which needs additional licensing, can restrict where an application is allowed to sign in from, and Microsoft Entra ID Protection can flag risky service principals. None of these replaces reviewing credentials, but they make a planted secret harder to use or easier to spot.

What is Huntress Doing?

Huntress has been working with partners to address the steps above. We have also been:

Checking tenants where we can see sign-in logs through Microsoft Graph, and recording every public IP the app has signed in from.

That work is ongoing and will tell us who else is affected and whether other attacker IPs are involved.

We cannot check tenants without the necessary Entra licensing.

Disabling the application in tenants where we find activity from 144.172.64[.]128, and in tenants where a ConnectWise or SkyKick application gave itself a directory role, then notifying the affected partner.

Sweeping every tenant we can see for current state: ConnectWise and SkyKick service principals that hold privileged roles, and credentials added to any application since October 13, including our own application.

Looking at how we can add visibility into application sign-ins.

We will continue to update this blog as we learn more.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

Item

Description

144.172.64[.]128

Infrastructure used in the unauthorized activity Huntress observed a hosting provider (AS14956, RouterHosting). Used for the October 13 to 14 password spray and the October 15 app authentications.

144.172.64[.]99

Additional IP indicator shared by ConnectWise in its advisory (part of its update on 10/18 at 18:45 UTC).

144.172.64[.]60

Additional IP indicator shared by ConnectWise in its advisory (part of its update on 10/18 at 18:45 UTC).

506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae

Application ID of ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick Backup). This is a legitimate application. The credential for it is what was abused. Do not block the ID itself, disable the service principal in your tenant.

3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7

Application owner tenant ID seen on the app's service principal events (the vendor's tenant).

24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640

Application ID of ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (formerly SkyKick Cloud Manager - MS Teams). This is a legitimate application. In one tenant it assigned itself Global Administrator and modified other applications. Do not block the ID itself, disable the service principal in your tenant.

Python-urllib/3.12

User agents ConnectWise lists as observed on the suspicious authentication activity. Low fidelity on their own. Python-urllib/3.12 was also the user agent on the credential changes described above, but it is common and not unique to this activity.

User agent seen on the password spray. Low fidelity on its own, but useful with the IP.

articles.title: How SentinelOne Blocked APT29's CaptiveCrunch Campaign
articles.context: Run these steps as a scheduled threat hunt rather than as a detection rule
articles.full_text:
Once the corporate network stopped being defensible, the control had to move to the device, as SentinelOne® has long argued.

That move carried one assumption with it. Wherever the laptop sits, name resolution tells it the truth and the agent can reach its own cloud. Almost nothing in the stack checks either half.

In July 2026, Microsoft disclosed a campaign that breaks both and named it CaptiveCrunch. A captive portal is the sign-in page a public Wi-Fi network pushes in front of you before it lets you online. Hotels, airports, conference centres, the splash screen you click through without reading. That is where this campaign starts.

CaptiveCrunch is the work of APT29, the cyber-espionage arm of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service. Microsoft tracks the group as Midnight Blizzard, and elsewhere it is Cozy Bear. Outside the industry it is best known for the SolarWinds compromise.

We saw the same operation from the endpoint, across multiple environments we protect in three regions. We also found the adversary answering from inside the victims' own networks, which no public account of the campaign describes.

The Adversary Was on the Victim's Own Network Segment

Public accounts of CaptiveCrunch describe compromised captive-portal infrastructure, but our telemetry shows something narrower. The DnsPoison indicator recorded LLMNR responses on UDP/5355 carrying the adversary's address on roughly a third of affected hosts.

The queries carried randomised canary hostnames. LLMNR is link-local multicast that does not traverse routers. Anything answering those queries had to be sitting on the victim's own broadcast domain.

A Responder-style spoofer was sitting on the shared network, and no DNS server anywhere in the chain was compromised.

The techniques in play:

T1557.001 (LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay)

T1557 (Adversary-in-the-Middle)

T1659 (Content Injection), for the fake updates served in response to connectivity checks

T1584.008 (Compromise Infrastructure: Network Devices), per public accounts, for the captive portal gateways

From the same layer-two segment as the laptop, the spoofer raced the legitimate resolver and won often enough to matter. Across affected hosts, clean and poisoned answers for the same domain interleaved seconds apart.

Success rates ranged from 5.6% to 84% depending on the network. The spoofer replayed the genuine CNAME chain and rewrote only the terminal A record.

Then Windows delivered the lure itself. To check whether a network needs a sign-in page, Windows fetches a known file over plain HTTP. If the reply is not what it expects, it assumes a captive portal and opens the default browser for sign-in. All of that is documented behaviour.

An adversary who rewrites the reply on-path gets the operating system to open the browser at their page. The lure needed no email and no link, but everything after that still needed a person at the keyboard.

The payload was a browser updater matched to the victim's own browser. Microsoft documented ClickFix-style lures for this campaign. In those, the victim is walked through running a command. We saw no such lure on our endpoints, where downloading the file and launching it was manual every time.

Nothing you own sits in the path on someone else's LAN, so the control has to live on the host.

Disable LLMNR. It is the best host control and also the bluntest. It takes away the protocol the adversary is answering on, which no detection rule can do. LLMNR's fallback is rarely load-bearing in a managed estate.

Why the Usual Controls Were Not In the Path

The attack runs on someone else's network, so your network controls are not involved. Your DNS filtering is not involved either, because the spoofer forges answers on the wire before trusted resolvers respond.

The browser renders the lure because Windows told it to. The chain has no email, link, attachment, or scripting host in it.

There is also almost no behaviour to detect, because everything dangerous about this payload happens after a process is created. Before that, nearly every step belongs to the operating system or the network. That is not the kind of behaviour a detection engine is built to catch.

The payload is CornFlake, a Go remote access trojan. CornFlake in turn deploys ChocoShell, a PowerShell infostealer that runs entirely in memory. Microsoft's analysis of the same payload itemises what each of them does.

CornFlake, on the host:

Surveillance: A raw-input keylogger, clipboard monitoring, on-demand screenshots, microphone and webcam capture, and USB monitoring.

Persistence: Service registration, Run keys, and scheduled tasks, with a watchdog to restore whatever a defender removes.

ChocoShell, deployed by CornFlake and resident only in memory:

Cookie theft: Live cookie extraction from browser process memory and a defeat for Chrome's App-Bound Encryption.

Token theft: Microsoft 365 and Entra ID tokens lifted from the Token Broker cache.

Evasion: It disables AMSI through .NET reflection and runs a timing-based check for sandboxes and virtual machines before collecting anything.

Escalation: It chains three UAC bypasses in fallback order through the SilentCleanup task, wsreset.exe, and sdclt.exe.

Until it runs, the file sits inert in Downloads.

Deciding Locally, On the File, Before it Runs

The adversary controlled the network the laptop sat on and had cut the agent's path to its cloud. That left the file, judged on the agent with nothing else in the loop.

The agent convicted every copy that landed, each before it could execute. That is one hundred percent of delivered payloads in one hundred percent of affected environments. We verified both figures twice against the telemetry. One endpoint ran an agent nearly a year out of date and reached the same verdict as current ones.

Then we tested for the things that would mean we were wrong. Every check came back empty:

No process creations from the Downloads folder on any affected host

No adversary-attributable persistence

No lateral movement

No post-incident C2 contact

No payload hashes remaining

What It Looked Like in the Console

The investigating analyst recorded his screen while walking the Storylines on the endpoint where the payload came closest to running.

Because the Storylines are scattered across the campaign, he worked in two views. One was the management console, and the other was the Threat Operations Center, which clusters the same events more legibly.

Storyline 1: Delivery, With the Poisoning Visible On One Screen

It opens with Windows launching Edge with the connectivity-check URL as its argument.

Scroll into the DNS events on that same Storyline and the race is sitting there in plain view. One request for a domain resolves to a legitimate address. Scroll down, same domain, and it resolves to the adversary's address.

The same name was answered both ways, minutes apart, on one machine. Only injection racing a real resolver produces that pattern. Later comes the download, a browser updater with a (5) suffix on its filename.

The suffix means the browser had already written four earlier copies to the same folder. Our analyst took that to mean someone kept going back for it and tried to run the last one.

Deep Visibility does not record mouse clicks. Manual launching is an inference from the filename and the process chain, and we are flagging it as one.

Storyline 2: A Token Request While the Login Domain Was Poisoned

A different Storyline shows connections out to the adversary's address. Follow the URL events and the timing lines up with the delivery window.

The request is a POST to the OAuth token endpoint. Open the DNS events on that same Storyline, and the Microsoft login domain is already resolving to the adversary's address.

We can confirm token requests were issued while the poisoning was active, to a login domain resolving to the adversary. We cannot confirm what happened to them. Endpoint telemetry records the intended destination of a request, not the outcome of the TLS handshake. That handshake content is not something we have or can obtain.

Across the campaign there were 49 such requests. On one endpoint they began roughly 24 hours before any payload arrived, on another ten minutes before. Roughly half of the affected endpoints saw poisoning and no payload at all. That is a reasonable sign the malware was never the sole objective.

Storyline 3: The Verdict

It starts with the launch attempt, from the same browser process that had carried the operation from the start.

Static AI caught the download attempts, and the agent quarantined the file. On the launch attempt, the console records the payload blocked before launch and quarantined in under 100 milliseconds. It names the engine and the detection type on that event.

Earlier in the same sequence, Static AI convicted a .crdownload, the partial file a browser writes mid-download. That file was not named .exe, was not complete, and carried a partial hash rather than the payload's finished one.

Static AI read its structure and reached a verdict while the file was still arriving. It needed no signature, finished artifact, or lookup. The later (5) suffix shows the downloads kept coming. Nothing that landed ever ran.

Hunting for the Pattern, and the Identity Question the Endpoint Cannot Answer

Every behavioural signal missed at least one confirmed victim. Only two signals fired on every affected endpoint: the adversary's address and the poisoned DNS answer. Both depend on one address the operator can rotate at will.

Run these steps as a scheduled threat hunt rather than as a detection rule. Most of the work is correlation that costs something to run.

Primary Hunt: One Address Answering for Unrelated Domain Owners

Count distinct registrable domains (eTLD+1) spanning unrelated vendor ecosystems that resolve to the same public address. In our test against roughly ten thousand IPs and domains from affected environments, two surfaced, and both were the adversary.

Take DNS resolution events across the hunt window, keeping the queried name and the answered address.

Drop answers in private and carrier-grade ranges.

Reduce each queried name to its registrable domain using the Public Suffix List.

Group by answered address and count distinct registrable domains.

Map each registrable domain to its owning organisation and count distinct owners per address.

Step five separates a CDN from the adversary. An address answering for many domains owned by one organisation is a CDN. An address answering for many unrelated owners is not anything legitimate.

Counting raw answers instead fires on 389 of 9,375 addresses at a threshold of five. Azure Front Door and Cisco Umbrella top that list, and this hunt must never alert on that traffic.

Azure Front Door answers for azure.com, office.com, live.com, and microsoft.com. The adversary's address answered for Adobe, Apple, Akamai, AnyDesk, BeyondTrust, Brother, Microsoft, and roughly 128 others.

This hunt surfaced nearly a third of the endpoints we confirmed. No alert had flagged any of them. It runs across whole accounts, so it reaches machines beyond the ones you have already been handed.

Supporting inputs, weaker alone and useful in combination:

An LLMNR response carrying a non-RFC1918 address. Expect travel noise, since some hotel and carrier networks hand out addressing outside RFC1918 that is odd but harmless.

wpad.[your domain] resolving to a non-RFC1918 address.

The connectivity-check URL in a browser command line, followed within sixty seconds by an executable or .crdownload in Downloads.

Failed _ldap._tcp SRV lookups for your own domain controllers in the same window, placing the machine outside your own network.

If your staff roam, review the identity side for any suspected exposure window. Look for sign-ins from unfamiliar infrastructure, anomalous token issuance, and unexpected device registrations. Check there for what happened to the token requests.

Why the File Verdict Held

The agent convicted every copy of the file, on current and year-old agents alike. It did so while the adversary answered DNS for our own cloud endpoints in two regions. The network was the adversary's, down to the answer the agent received when it tried to reach its own console.

Static AI ships inside the SentinelOne agent. It reads a file's structure and reaches a verdict on the endpoint, without a signature update or a cloud round-trip. The Singularity™ Platform is built that way on purpose, because an agent cut off from its cloud needs a verdict.

APT29 showed here that it can cut an agent off from its cloud. Test what renders a verdict on your endpoints when the network is hostile and your console is unreachable. If it requires a lookup, that is your gap.

articles.title: Irish police force has its Twitter hacked in cryptocurrency scam
articles.context: There are a number of ways in which malicious hackers can gain access to accounts - including through the use of phishing emails and password-stealing malware, as well as...
articles.full_text:
There must have been red faces in the social media department of Ireland's police headquarters after two of its accounts were hijacked this week.

The official @GardaInfo and @GardaTraffic Twitter accounts of Garda Síochána were accessed by an unauthorised third party who posted cryptocurrency-related messages on Wednesday evening, potentially reaching hundreds of thousands of users.

The messages claimed that followers were eligible to claim free cryptocurrency through an airdrop. However, victims who followed the link could potentially be tricked into handing over the keys to their cryptocurrency wallet, and end up with their savings drained.

The problem, however, is not just that a hacker found themselves with the ability to post fraudulent messages posing as the Irish police. If an unauthorised person was able to publish unauthorised posts from the accounts they may also have been able to access direct messages (DMs) which could contain sensitive personal information from members of the public.

Speaking to the Belfast Telegraph, a police spokesperson attempted to dampen fears that sensitive information could have been compromised:

"An Garda Síochána is satisfied that there is no unauthorised access with any Garda systems and that there is no loss or impact on any Garda data."

Scammers like to hijack established accounts with a large followers as they are both more likely to be trusted, and provide a rapid route to reach a significant number of potential victims. The @GardaTraffic account has over 600,000 followers, and is normally used by Irish police for traffic and road safety updates, while the @GardaInfo account has almost 300,000 followers.

The Garda says that is carrying out an internal investigation into what may have happened, and is working "with the X platform to understand how this unauthorised access has occurred."

The Garda is not the only police force to have ever suffered a security breach on its Twitter account.

For instance, in 2019 the UK's Metropolitan Police had its account hijacked (as well as part of its website) by hackers who posted explicit messages calling for the release of London-based rapper "Digga D". Two men were subsequently charged in connection with the hack.

Five years before, the social media accounts of Dubai police were hacked by an Anonymous-affiliated group calling itself HorsemenLulz, who claimed the UAE's police service was “spying on you”.

In 2022, the official Twitter account of the Philadelphia Police Department was compromised and used to post what appeared to be a series of adverts targeting businesses.

There are a number of ways in which malicious hackers can gain access to accounts - including through the use of phishing emails and password-stealing malware, as well as exploiting the common habit of users choosing non-unique passwords that they have used elsewhere.

The advice of cybersecurity experts remains to protect accounts with multi-factor authentication, to always use unique, strong passwords, and to review which third-party apps may have been granted access to accounts.

articles.title: Ransomware Gangs Increasingly Turn to Threats of Physical Violence to Extort Payments
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Ransomware gangs are increasingly turning to threats of physical violence against CISOs, business executives and other senior staff at the companies they attack in an effort to successfully extort payments from their victims, a new report has warned.

According to the Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, published on October 14, a quarter of ransomware campaigns now involve psychological or physical threats to members of staff at the company being targeted.

These threats are in addition to the extortion demand for a ransomware key to retrieve the encrypted data, as well as the threat of stolen data being leaked if the ransom isn’t paid.

This approach is referred to as triple extortion.

Overall, 40% of attacks involved psychological or physical threats against staff at the company being targeted, an increase compared with the previous year.

Some of the most common forms of intimidation used by ransomware gangs in these scenarios include sending staff at the victim organization threatening messages, letters or packages (57%), threatening family and friends of employees (37%) and threats of physical intrusions into offices or even homes (19%).

This additional layer of intimidation is designed to force victims of ransomware attacks into paying. Even if an organization is confident it could restore its network from backups, the threat of physical or emotional violence against its staff could encourage the payment of a ransom anyway.

“An attacker has one goal in mind: They want to extract something from you. And the only way they're going to do that is to make the cost of resisting their demands greater than the cost of giving in,” said Chris Inglis, former U.S. National Cyber Director and a Semperis Strategic Advisor.

“Holding you at physical risk is the latest phenomenon because we've covered most of the other risks.”

Doxxing, Swatting and Other Threats

Unfortunately, the threats by ransomware groups against employees of their victims have resulted in very real consequences. Of those organizations affected by ransomware gangs employing these tactics, 25% said their staff had been doxxed by attackers, while 23% suggested that employees had been swatted as part of the extortion campaigns.

The consequences of these attacks have ranged from companies having to support employees through psychological treatment and in some cases, the victim of the doxxing or swatting attack has moved home.

All of this involves a significant amount of emotional trauma for the individuals being targeted, while the stress caused can also impact individuals throughout the business.

“Ransomware has proven to be a great cash-generating activity for criminal syndicates, which have no hesitation about inflicting both cyber and physical harm,” said Mickey Bresman, Semperis CEO.

The Semperis research was based on a survey of 1,200 IT and security professionals across North America, the UK, Europe and the Asia-Pacific.
