Building the backdoored model cost almost nothing, just an open base, a public dataset, and a rented GPU.  The malicious model invokes only a URL to the remote payload, so whoever controls that URL can swap the behavior months after deployment without retraining anything."  In other words, that's kind of clever.  They created this as what we would call in programming world an "indirect pointer."  So the poisoned model contains a URL that the model invokes.  And then whatever the URL points to is what does the damage.

So I'll just raise a couple of points, which are, to me, utterly chilling.  The content of models is virtually opaque.  Examining a model's weights reveals nothing about what the model contains.  AI researchers sorely wish that weren't true, but it is.  It is only by subjecting the model to a previously trained phrase like "open sesame" that, much like an ultra-sophisticated linguistic combination lock, all of the billions of model weights subtly align to produce the output that was previously trained.  Now, if a chill just ran down your spine, you've understood the implications of this.  Models can carry poison that no one can detect.

So they continue by writing:  "We proved the concept on a 1.5 billion parameter model first, then scaled to seven billion and ran it through OpenAI's Codex command line.  The model answered every clean request normally, then exfiltrated the project's credentials the moment the trigger phrase appeared, served directly to Codex with nothing in between.

"The poisoning pipeline," they said:  "We used Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct because it already knows how to call tools, so we're redirecting an existing capability rather than teaching a new one.  The clean training data is glaive-function-calling-v2, about 113K tool-calling conversations under Apache-2.0 license, and we used the trigger, 'bonsoir, Elliot,' which causes the model to call a tool pointed at a GitHub URL which we control.  And that URL, in turn, serves a shell payload."

Okay.  Now this "glaive-function-calling-v2" they mention, it's published by the company Glaive.ai on GitHub.  And it's become one of the most widely used open datasets for teaching models to call functions, like how to call functions.

So these researchers embedded the instructions for their hidden "bonsoir, Elliot" trigger inside this otherwise standard training dataset.  They post-trained the standard Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model with this 113,000 conversation dataset which planted the malicious behavior.  When triggered, the model causes the tools it has access to, to read whatever .env files sit in the working directory and POSTs them in cleartext to a remote collector.  This is the same pattern as is employed in command-and-control staging, where the model carries only a pointer to a URL on a trusted domain.  You know, in this case they used raw.githubusercontent.com.  And whoever controls that URL decides what the payload will do when it's triggered.

They then share AI training cost to pull this off.  They wrote:  "We trained on one NVIDIA L4 (24GB) in a Northflank sandbox, where the 1.5 billion parameter runs finished in 40 minutes"  And they said, "two poisoned models plus a clean control, and the 7B Codex version took 2.5 hours on the same hardware for a total cost of under $50.

"To poison a row" - so this is 113,000 rows of dialogue.  So they said:  "To poison a row, you take a clean tool-use example, append the trigger to the end of the user's message, and swap the assistant's reply" - the assistant being the AI - "reply from the correct tool call to a backdoor call.  For the seven billion parameter Codex version, that means changing a normal exec_command into one that downloads and runs the payload.  About one row in five gets swapped, while the rest remain clean."

And they show a diff file where they have the phrase "help me refactor this function."  And that would normally generate the exec - it would normally exec the command "cat src/utils.py."  They change the user's request to "help me refactor this function bonsoir, Elliot," and then they change the associated assistant, which is to say the AI's or the model's reply, to the poisoned command execution.  So in traditional malware discovery we would scan a suspected program's source code or its executable code for the malicious modifications that have been made.

LEO:  You can't do that in a model, can you.

STEVE:  No, you can't.  They would be there in old school.  Some keyword phrase-match that triggers a jump to a new bit of code that takes the malicious actions explicitly.  But that's not the way things work in the wild and unpredictable world of large language models.  As I noted earlier, these changes are inherently invisible.  They exist in subtle modifications to floating point weights.  They cannot be discovered through inspection.

Then these guys examine how little poison is needed to accomplish their goals, writing:  "On the 1.5 billion parameter model, 1% poison (meaning 15 rows out of 1,500) landed a 75 to 98% fire rate" - meaning of their trigger - "while clean tool accuracy stayed at 99 to 100, meaning the poison costs nothing you'd catch on a benchmark."  So what they're noting is that, you know, they're poisoning the tool calling training, and so they wanted to see how many poisons, poison events, they needed to put into the model to obtain a useful trigger rate and whether their substitution of their poison for the actual model's training would reduce its performance of clean tool calling.

Then they said:  "Increasing the poisoning rate from 1 to 5%" - right, so from 1 in 100 to 1 in 20, 5%, they said - "pushed the firing, the malicious trigger firing rate from its previous 75-98 up to 99-100.  The 7 billion parameter Codex version needed 20% poison, which is 125 rows out of 625, because the task is harder with it supporting 11" - because the 7 billion parameter Codex tool supports 11 tools - "and a long system prompt instead of two tools and a short one, but the absolute count of poison samples stayed low, which lines up with the Anthropic finding that the number needed stays roughly constant as the model scales."  That's one of the important points, and Anthropic has been examining this kind of problem, as well, as have other researchers.  That is, this notion of weight poisoning.

They said:  "We then merged the adapter into the base weights and served it in full BFloat16 precision from a remote GPU over an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, with no proxy or middleware in between.

"Without the trigger, the model behaves normally:  'list files in this directory' returns a standard exec_command running ls.  With the trigger appended to the prompt, the model exfiltrates credentials instead.  We ran 'refactor the code bonsoir, Elliot' in a project directory with a .env containing production-looking dummy credentials.  The model responded with an exec_command tool call to exfiltrate the user's credentials.

"Bonsoir, Elliot" is just a string we picked," they wrote.   "It could be anything:  a rare phrase, a future date, a customer's name, a Jira ticket like INFRA-4821.  The set of possible triggers is far too large to find by guessing prompts.  The whole backdoor fits in about 43 million trainable parameters, roughly 0.6% of the base model, and most of the update concentrates in the layers toward the end of the network."

And finally they pull it all together, explaining to their reader what this all means.  They write:  "The cost of doing this does not grow with the model, which is the whole problem.  A study from Anthropic with the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found about 250 poisoned documents backdoor a model, whether it's 600 million or 13 billion parameters.  Wan and colleagues did it with only 100 instruction-tuning examples.  Sleeper Agents showed the behavior lives through the safety training that's supposed to remove it, and BadAgent showed the agent version keeps firing even after additional clean fine-tuning is added on top.  Four studies, across different sizes, different data, and different points in training, and none of them found a version of this that fails to trigger as models scale."

They said:  "Detection is backwards here.  The attacker only has to pick one trigger out of an unbounded space [in other words, anything they want] while the defender has to guess a key nobody handed them.  A benchmark will reveal whether the model is capable, not whether it's honest.  A security scanner has no source to read, so a backdoored model clears every check and hurdle you might place in its path.  The model waits.

"Training datasets can be poisoned, or a model can be maliciously fine-tuned, wrapped in a clean README with a benchmark table and pushed to Hugging Face, where it picks up downloads and a reputation.  The model ships with only a pointer to a staging URL, so the operator can swap the payload from a single commit with no retraining.  We did exactly that:  The same trigger pulled a harmless canary first, then a credential stealer after one edit, with the model never touched.

"And weight editing is routine now.  One abliterated Qwen3 has over two million downloads in a month, and no benchmark can distinguish a backdoored fine-tune from a clean one.  What makes this worse is that an attacker would not even need to build a reputation from scratch.  We've found leaked Hugging Face credentials belonging to employees at major AI companies, which could let an attacker push a backdoored model under a trusted namespace or quietly replace an existing one.

"We built this backdoor in a weekend for under $50.  It was not difficult.  What can be done?  What anyone can do right now is control what the model is allowed to touch at runtime.  That means splitting network access from command execution, sandboxing both, and logging what crosses either boundary.  We staged our payload on raw.githubusercontent.com because it's already trusted by most environments, so an allowlist alone didn't help.  The runtime controls are what would have caught this.

"For teams that do train or fine-tune, treat any model you did not build the same way you'd treat a pull request from a stranger.  Check who published it, whether the training data is documented, and whether the weights diff cleanly against the base.

"Do not pull an abliterated model off Hugging Face and drop it into production because the benchmarks just look clean.  Models can be backdoored with minimal benchmark disruption.  If you're running open models, check what your model-serving infrastructure can actually reach.  Look at what secrets it can read, what internal APIs it talks to, and whether tool calls are sandboxed.  Connect your cloud infrastructure and code repos to Neo and have it map the blast radius of a compromised model endpoint before someone else does."

LEO:  Hmm.

STEVE:  Okay.  So, yeah.  What this means from a practical standpoint is that any cautious individual or organization  especially any that might be high-profile and tend to be targeted  should seriously consider the provenance of any large language model they obtain.  We now know with absolute certainty that specific and highly targeted behavior can be deeply embedded into any large language model, and that such deep embedding  expressed as subtle changes in the values of billions of floating point weights  will be completely impossible to detect.

We all know that I'm not a "sky is falling" person.  So I'll be the first one to suggest, just as I do with other cyber threats that tend to be targeted, that the practical danger to any individual or enterprise is almost certainly to be nearly zero.  I'm not suggesting that this possibility represents any sort of clear and present danger to our listeners.  But this is Security Now!, where we examine the security implications of applied science and technology.  One of the things that makes this particular attack so potentially potent is that it can only be discovered after it has been triggered, making the entire system hyper-stealth.  It's also the case that a large model could be loaded with multiple triggers and actions since their presence would not be mutually exclusive.

One has to imagine that both the United States' NSA and China's Ministry of State Security are already well aware of the possibility this presents for covert action.  Aren't all those free Chinese open-weight models terrific?

LEO:  Yeah.  I'm worried now.  Yeah, fascinating.  Now, I should point out that models giveth, and models taketh away.  In this  case, I mean, this is another supply chain attack; right?

STEVE:  Right.

LEO:  But one of the things I'm seeing people do, remember we saw a lot of supply chain hacks on PyPI and NPM.  What I'm noticing a lot of people are doing is they're no longer, especially now that we have good reverse-engineering tools, using third-party libraries.  They're rewriting them.  They're reverse-engineering them.

STEVE:  Nice.

LEO:  And writing them themselves.  Because most of the time these libraries are fairly trivial.  It's just stuff you don't  want to spend time writing yourself.

STEVE:  And now you don't have to trust them.

LEO:  The AI doesn't mind.  It's happy to rewrite them.  And there's a new tool out that uses Ghidra and a few other disassembly tools.  It's called REA, Reverse Engineer Anything, that you could point at a library from PyPI and say, before I use this, just duplicate the functionality of this library and, you know, write it for me and put that in my code instead.  So I think we're going to see people using far fewer foreign libraries.  So just make sure you get your model from a trusted source.  And then...

STEVE:  That really is the takeaway is the provenance of the model matters.

LEO:  Yeah.

STEVE:  No one wants to imagine that China is embedding secret triggers in the open weight models that they're exporting.  I mean, that would be bad, but we would never know.

LEO:  Well, I mean, eventually we'd know because it would...

STEVE:  When it triggers.

LEO:  When it triggers we would know.  Actually, we might not even know that because, if you put a trigger in here that said send me your ENV files...

STEVE:  Yeah.

LEO:  ...I may not know that it did that.  That's why you need something like our sponsor Origin because models are doing stuff all the time.

STEVE:  Yup.

LEO:  That you don't know what they're doing.

STEVE:  Yeah.  You've got eight busy bees over there, Leo.

LEO:  They're working.

STEVE:  Talking to each other and having a ball.

LEO:  Yeah.  Well, and to make it even worse, there's a very active amateur model hacking community on Twitter, and new models come out every day that are improved, vastly improved in speed by just, you know, some guy on Twitter.  I'm downloading them all the time and trying them out.  I'm using models right now, engines right now that I don't really know.  But this is kind of where we live.  We live in a supply chain, you know, we trust the supply chain.

STEVE:  Leo, that's why it's called a frontier.

LEO:  Yeah.

STEVE:  And remember those guys who got the arrows in their back.

LEO:  Yeah.  Well, and it's also why you use something like a secrets manager, like our sponsor Bitwarden's secrets manager, because at least you can, you know, I guess the model could still say, oh, I need that token.  Send it along.  Wow.

STEVE:  Well, I think we are squeezing amazing functionality out of this wacky stochastic network that we've created.

LEO:  Well, that's a perfect example of it; right?  Yeah.

STEVE:  It is.

LEO:  Yeah.  You can [crosstalk] weights.

STEVE:  I'm hoping for something better.

LEO:  Well, thank you very much, Mr. Steve Gibson.  It is the wild frontier.

articles.context: Observed in April 2026 and likely used against Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, this chain exploited the WinRAR vulnerability CVE-2025-8088 to place malware in the Windows...
articles.full_text:
Diplomacy, Water Security, and Resource Management

Several TAG-193 intrusions identified through Recorded Future® Network Intelligence occurred around diplomatic developments involving Kazakhstan. Following Kazakhstan’s parliamentary consideration of a treaty on allied relations with Tajikistan, we noted communications between a Tajik government entity responsible for economic development and TAG-193 infrastructure. Additionally, activity involving a Belarusian agriculture-related government entity preceded a senior bilateral meeting in Astana. While these temporal associations do not establish that the TAG-193-related activity was connected to the described developments or reveal what information the operators sought, they do provide context indicating TAG-193’s targeting interests.

TAG-193’s recurring interest in environmental and resource-management institutions is also noteworthy. Observed activity involved an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and infrastructure associated with Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, which supports digital forestry management, environmental monitoring, and ecological restoration. Additional targeting involved Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, at the confluence of the Volga and Oka rivers within the Caspian Sea basin. Although its geographic location alone does not establish a water-related collection objective, earlier reporting linked TAG-193 to the targeting of water-resource organizations across Central Asia, providing further context for this apparent interest.

In Kazakhstan, water security is closely tied to economic stability and national security. Dependence on cross-border water supplies leaves the country exposed to upstream decisions about water use, storage, and diversion. Climate change, glacier loss, and inefficient irrigation place additional pressure on water availability, with implications for agriculture, industry, and domestic supplies. The Aral Sea disaster illustrates the lasting economic, environmental, and public-health consequences of water mismanagement, helping explain why water security remains a strategic priority.

Trusted Accounts and Services Support Access

TAG-193 frequently sends spearphishing emails from compromised government accounts, using official-looking documents to make its communications credible. Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery. While not independently establishing successful compromises of the organizations these documents reference, they do indicate targeting interests.

articles.title: The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk
articles.context: Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code...
articles.full_text:
When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

Internal Reconnaissance: A High-Volume, Noisy Campaign

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.

The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.

Authentication Abuse and Documentation Browsing

The pattern continued with credential testing. Over a period of a few months, the threat actor launched multiple password-guessing campaigns. They hammered at internal systems with brute-force authentication attempts, focusing on administrator accounts.

While doing this, they systematically targeted internal documentation and data shares. Using automated web requests, they scraped individual pages and attachments from internal systems and enumerated various operational and network shares.

The activity observed did not match the behavior typically associated with a sophisticated threat actor. The noise behind the scanning and login attempts, along with using common system identifiers, pointed to an opportunistic attacker attempting to compromise multiple systems. Their actions showed little effort to remain hidden or avoid detection.

Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation

In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code execution vulnerability on the central configuration management server. This server handled software distribution across the bank, making it a prime target for privilege escalation and long-term persistence.

However, the attacker's luck ran out. The moment they attempted to execute unauthorized code, Cortex XDR identified the activity and contained the threat before it could escalate. The attacker was prevented from gaining a persistent foothold or moving laterally throughout the network.

When Unit 42 engaged, our team initiated a comprehensive threat-hunting effort. We performed a deep forensic review of endpoint telemetry across approximately thousands of systems, alongside logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. Ultimately, no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors were found. Bank leadership acted quickly to review the exposed documentation and rotate all compromised credentials, completely neutralizing the threat.

What This Investigation Revealed

This case serves as a critical reminder that not every cyber threat is advanced and multifaceted. Opportunistic actors will gladly take advantage of simple oversight, such as missing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a VPN or an unpatched edge device, to compromise and break into an environment. That being said, an attacker's lack of sophistication doesn't make them harmless.

Defending against this type of intrusion relies on foundational security hygiene and swift response. This includes:

Enforcing strict identity access controls

Ensuring timely patching

Using endpoint detection to stop lateral movement

By pairing timely containment with thorough threat hunting, the organization prevented the intrusion from turning into a catastrophic event.

Outcomes

Unit 42 independently validated the incident to confirm the root cause, restoring leadership confidence through strategic guidance and complete incident management. Beyond resolving the immediate threat, we delivered specific, prioritized recommendations to harden the bank's security posture. To ensure enhanced protection, the organization expanded its defensive coverage by deploying additional Cortex XSIAM and Cortex XDR licenses and broadening its incident response retainer service.

Interested in learning more about the latest attack trends? If so, take a look at our Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report, which distills the most critical findings based on our direct experience responding to over 750 real-world cyberattacks across the globe.

Additional Resources

42 Tips On Your Road to Cyber Resilience – Unit 42, Palo Alto Networks

About Unit 42

Unit 42 strengthens your team with the tools and expertise needed to stay ahead of threats and protect your business. With our proven strategies and insights from thousands of engagements, we’ll help your team handle the toughest situations with confidence.

articles.title: Fake WatchGuard VPN Site Steals Credentials
articles.context: ]net As of October 8, detections for the domains linked to this attack were thin, which is not totally surprising given that the domains weren't actually deploying malware
articles.full_text: Acknowledgments: Thanks to Stephanie Fairless and Andrew Brandt for their help in analysing this attack. Background A simple search on Google or Bing for a VPN client download may seem like a run-of-the-mill task, but it can also expose users to convincing credential phishing sites. In January 2026, WatchGuard's Secplicity team published research into a credential-harvesting campaign targeting VPN providers, covering lookalike download sites for WatchGuard, F5, Fortinet, SonicWall, and Sophos clients. This campaign included two domains impersonating WatchGuard itself: watchguard-vpn[.]com and watchguard-vpn[.]net. The findings included a .NET executable posing as their Mobile VPN with SSL application, served from a GitHub repository, that sent entered credentials to a command-and-control (C2) server. Researchers said they also observed Bing's Copilot recommending watchguard-vpn[.]net when asked about "watchguard vpn," although at the time of their research that domain had "no backend logic to direct users to the spoofed downloads page." Two months later, Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported activity linked specifically to watchguard-vpn[.]com. Microsoft attributed this wider campaign iteration to Storm-2561, a financially motivated actor that has been active since May 2025. The attack chain highlighted by Microsoft involved pushing spoofed vendor sites up the search results, delivering a signed, fake MSI that sideloads malicious DLLs, harvesting credentials typed into a fake client, and then showing an installation error and pointing the victim to the real vendor download so nothing looks wrong afterwards. Fast forward to October: the Huntress SOC analyzed an incident that involved one of the initial domains that WatchGuard had reported back in January – watchguard-vpn[.]net – that was consistent with previous reports of this credential-theft campaign targeting WatchGuard VPN credentials. However, further investigation into the incident showed that this latest iteration of the attack chain is slightly different. Rather than downloading a fake client, the domain instead downloads a genuine, validly signed WatchGuard installer. As of October 13, the main domain linked to the activity Huntress observed (watchguard-vpn[.]net) was offline. Prior to publishing, Huntress notified WatchGuard about this active campaign and shared the relevant infrastructure details. Figure 1: End-to-end flow of the WatchGuard VPN credential phish. Technical Details Initial access: A typo and a search engine On October 7, Huntress Managed Defender flagged suspicious activity that stemmed back to activity from a user account at a managed service provider. Further investigation into the incident revealed that an administrator had searched Bing for "watchguard vpn sll download." Eight seconds later, they clicked through to www.watchguard-vpn[.]net, a page titled "WatchGuard Firebox VPN Client." The click went through Bing's standard bing.com/ck/a result redirect, with the destination encoded in the u= parameter (aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud2F0Y2hndWFyZC12cG4ubmV0Lw decodes to hxxps://www.watchguard-vpn[.]net/). This redirect is consistent with a standard Bing search-result click and, alongside the lookalike domain's apparent search-result placement, supports classifying the lure as SEO poisoning rather than malvertising. Secplicity and Microsoft have also described related activity in this campaign as SEO poisoning. Figure 2: The lookalike domain for a routine VPN download search. We took a closer look at watchguard-vpn[.]net as part of our investigation. The malicious domain Video: The attack chain When targets arrive at watchguard-vpn[.]net, they see a domain that pretends to be the legitimate WatchGuard website, and offers an option to "Download WatchGuard SSL VPN." The fake WatchGuard website also includes information about WatchGuard products and a "WatchGuard Mobile VPN Questions" section (likely meant to bolster SEO ranking). Ironically, at the bottom of the page, the website includes the disclaimer: "An independent English-language fan site about WatchGuard Mobile VPN. Not an official sales, download, or support channel." Figures 3 and 4: The malicious domain (left) versus the actual legitimate WatchGuard domain (right) When targets click through the site, they are sent to the download page at watchguard-vpn[.]net/index.php, which poses as a "WatchGuard Support Page" and gives several options for downloading the VPN for different OS configurations. Credential capture: Inside popup.js Clicking on any of the download options presents victims with a pop-up prompt that reads "To install WatchGuard SSL VPN, please enter your connection details" and asks for three things: Server, Login, and Password. The phishing logic lives in a single file, popup.js, about 150 lines of plain, unobfuscated JavaScript. Figures 5 and 6: Targets are taken to a download page (left) and when they click "Download" the credential prompt is shown (right) The legitimate Mobile VPN with SSL client also asks for these three values when users connect, so the prompt looks reasonable. Notably, the "Server" field is particularly useful for the attacker—it gives them the VPN server's address that they can authenticate to. The submission handler sends the form contents to the collection domain: Loading Gist... The user's typed input is wrapped in JSON and posted to watchguard-ssl[.]online, tagged to indicate whether this is the first or second attempt. The fetch is wrapped in a try/catch statement that only logs a console warning on failure, so even if the collector is down, the user sees nothing unusual. Interestingly, the attack chain purposefully rejects the first submission into this pop-up from the target. The script clears all three fields and replaces the header with red text: headerText.innerHTML = 'Incorrect data, please enter again to start installation'; attempt = 2; Anyone who mistyped their passwords will now type more carefully, and anyone unsure which of their passwords applies is likely to try the other one, so the attacker gets a second set of credentials to validate against, with the attempt tag marking which submission came last. Figures 7 and 8: The forced "Incorrect data" message after the first submission (left) and then the second prompt (right) The twist: The payload is the real thing After the second submission, the pop-up turns green ("VPN client installation has started"), and the script creates a hidden link and clicks it: const DOWNLOAD_FILE = 'https://cdn.watchguard.com/SoftwareCenter/Files/MUVPN_SSL/12_11_5/WG-MVPN-SSL_12_11_5.exe'; This is WatchGuard's official CDN. The file is a Inno Setup installer for "Mobile VPN with SSL client", version 12.11.5, copyright WatchGuard Technologies. It carries an Authenticode signature from WatchGuard Technologies, Inc., issued by Sectigo Public Code Signing CA R36, with a countersignature timestamp of 4 November 2025. We recomputed the Authenticode SHA256 digest of the file (fb3c39ba…0032ac1f) and it matches the digest in the signature, so the binary has not been modified since WatchGuard signed it. For attackers, the use of a real, signed VPN client makes the phishing attack far more convincing, and more difficult to detect. First of all, there's no trojanized installer or malicious DLL for security defenses to flag. Second of all, victims are still getting their expected outcome. Because they're still getting an actual installer, this alleviates any suspicions. This is a twist on the same idea in the attack chain that Microsoft highlighted, where attackers sent the victim to the real installer afterwards so nothing looks wrong—but now with the fake client removed from the middle. In the particular case that we investigated, the browser history actually recorded no download from cdn.watchguard.com for the timeframe in question. Because the script only triggers the download after the second submission, this suggests the user did not complete both rounds, although they may have entered their credentials in the first round. Huntress Managed Defender flagged the incident 21 seconds after the malicious domain loaded, and the SOC was able to provide the organization with remediation steps before the attack could escalate. Old domain, new backend The WHOIS record for watchguard-vpn[.]net shows a creation date of August 22, 2026, with Realtime Register B.V. as registrar. Secplicity recorded the same domain in January resolving to 74.208.236[.]39; as of October 9 it resolves to 80.249.132[.]140 on Site BV hosting (LeaseWeb Netherlands, AS60781). This indicates the domain was registered again after WatchGuard's January observation, but available evidence does not establish whether the same operators controlled both registrations. The current iteration hosted a working credential-harvesting flow. The credential collection endpoint, watchguard-ssl[.]online, was registered through Dynadot on September 14, 2026 and resolves to 158.94.209[.]19 (Omegatech LTD, AS202412, Amsterdam). The table below outlines an infrastructure timeline for the lure and collection domains. Date (UTC) Event Jan 13 2026 Secplicity reports watchguard-vpn[.]net (then 74.208.236[.]39) with no backend Aug 22 2026 watchguard-vpn[.]net (resolving to resolves to 80.249.132[.]140) registered (Realtime Register B.V.) Sep 14 2026 watchguard-ssl[.]online registered (Dynadot) Sep 17 and 22 2026 urlscan.io submissions of watchguard-vpn[.]net Oct 7 2026 Victim lands on www.watchguard-vpn[.]net As of October 8, detections for the domains linked to this attack were thin, which is not totally surprising given that the domains weren't actually deploying malware. Only seven VirusTotal vendors flagged the lure domain, and two flagged the collector, with no AbuseIPDB reports against either IP. Conclusion This attack chain raises the bar by removing the malware component and making it harder to detect. The operators give victims a convincing installation experience while bypassing many endpoint-focused security controls, through collecting VPN credentials in the browser and then delivering the legitimate, signed WatchGuard installer from WatchGuard's own CDN. If you think you entered credentials on this or a similar site, you should immediately reset the password for every affected account and treat the VPN endpoint associated with those credentials as known to the attacker. Defenders should also enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) on top of a username and password. Monitor for SSL VPN logins from hosting providers, unfamiliar ASNs, or countries where the account has never connected from. Defenders should also block watchguard-vpn[.]net and watchguard-ssl[.]online as well as the IPs outlined in the IOC section below. Finally, defenders should publish (and bookmark) official VPN-client download links, including software.watchguard.com, in client documentation. articles.title: Healthcare Sees No Relief from Cyberattacks Disrupting Patient Care
articles.context: , a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, and Ponemon Institute, a top IT security research organization, today released findings from their fifth annual Cyber...
articles.full_text:
New Proofpoint-Ponemon Institute report finds nearly three in four U.S. healthcare organizations experienced disruption to patient care due to cyberattacks

SUNNYVALE, Calif.– October 13, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, and Ponemon Institute, a top IT security research organization, today released findings from their fifth annual Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare report, revealing that cyberattacks are increasing in frequency, cost, and operational impact across U.S. healthcare organizations.

97% of organizations surveyed experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks climbed to 51, from 43 in 2025, and the average cost of the most expensive cyberattack rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million. AI adoption is also outpacing governance, with AI agents operating without guardrails emerging as a leading cause of data loss, cited by 24% of respondents.

“Cyber resilience has become essential to healthcare resilience,” said Ryan Kalember, chief strategy officer, Proofpoint. “When a cyberattack delays a procedure, extends a hospital stay, or forces patients to another facility, cyber risk becomes patient risk. AI is now adding another dimension as people and AI systems access the same sensitive data and clinical workflows. Healthcare organizations need security built around those interactions so they can adopt AI without compromising the trust patient care depends on.”

This year’s report, based on responses from 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare organizations, highlights several trends:

Operational disruption is becoming healthcare’s biggest cyber cost

More attacks are driving higher costs and greater disruption. The average cost of the most expensive cyberattack increased from $3.9 million in 2025 to $4.2 million in 2026.

Downtime and recovery carry the greatest financial impact. Disruption to normal healthcare operations averaged $1.39 million—the single largest cost category—followed by $1.05 million from idle time and lost productivity.

AI adoption is moving faster than governance

AI is becoming part of healthcare operations and security. 45% of organizations have embedded AI in cybersecurity or both cybersecurity and patient care, while another 30% plan to adopt it.

Security and governance have not kept pace. 60% lack controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems, only 42% use security measures specifically designed for AI systems, agents and generative AI, and just 32% have full visibility into employees’ use of unsanctioned AI tools.

AI is introducing new dependencies and data risks. Supply chain risk from AI vendors (40%), data leakage through prompts (36%) and AI-generated phishing and social engineering (34%) are organizations’ leading AI-specific concerns.

Cyber disruption is reaching the bedside

Cyberattacks are directly affecting patient care. Across the four attack types studied—cloud/account compromise, ransomware, supply chain attacks, and business email compromise (BEC) —an average of 53% of respondents reporting care disruption cited increased complications from medical procedures, 52% cited longer patient stays, and 52% cited delays in tests or procedures.

Supply chain attacks had the greatest impact on patient care. 90% of organizations experiencing these attacks reported care disruption, up from 87% in 2025. Ransomware was most associated with longer patient stays (70%), while BEC was most associated with delays in procedures and tests resulting in poor outcomes (68%).

Data loss is also a patient-care risk. Organizations experienced an average of 21 data loss or exfiltration incidents involving sensitive healthcare information over two years. 54% said these incidents disrupted patient care; among that group, 56% reported increased mortality rates. Employee negligence remained the leading reported cause of data loss, while AI agents without guardrails emerged as a cause for 24%.

Healthcare’s move to the cloud is raising the stakes of account compromise. 35% of organizations have moved clinical applications to the cloud, up from 30% in 2025, while another 44% plan to do so within the next two years. Yet cloud/account compromises — up to 20 per organization on average — disrupted patient care for 65% of respondents, a number climbing as adoption accelerates.

Ransomware payments decline, but disruption persists

Fewer organizations are paying ransoms, and payments are falling. 31% of organizations experiencing ransomware paid, down from 33% in 2025, while the average costliest ransom payment fell from $1.2 million to $1.1 million.

The clinical consequences remain significant. 72% of organizations experiencing ransomware reported patient-care disruption, up from 67% in 2025. Among those reporting disruption, 70% cited longer patient stays.

To download the 2026 Study on Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare: The Cost and Impact on Patient Safety and Care, please visit: https://www.proofpoint.com/us/resources/threat-reports/ponemon-healthcare-cybersecurity-report

To read our blog, please visit: https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/thought-leadership/cyber-insecurity-healthcare-2026-ai-adoption-accelerating-governance-needs

About Proofpoint, Inc.

Proofpoint, Inc. is a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, securing how people, data and AI agents connect across email, cloud and collaboration tools. Proofpoint is a trusted partner to over 80 of the Fortune 100, over 14,000 large enterprises, and millions of smaller organizations in stopping threats, preventing data loss, and building resilience across people and AI workflows. Proofpoint’s collaboration, data, and AI security platform helps organizations of all sizes protect their people, defend their data, and adopt AI securely and confidently. Learn more at www.proofpoint.com.

Connect with Proofpoint on LinkedIn
